text:
Qwen3.8-27B hitting 381 tok/s on a single RTX 3090 sounds amazing 

But the real thing isn’t the GPU.

It’s teaching the inference engine to stop predicting information it already has.

The setup uses Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 speculative decoding, context lookup, longer verification blocks, prefix caching, quantized KV cache and optimized verification.

DFlash2 normally drafts around 7 tokens.

Here, the system can verify up to 16 positions by using tokens already present in the context.

On a 25K-token document reproduction workload:

DFlash2: ~260 tok/s
Optimized verification: ~382 tok/s

The reported acceptance rate reached roughly 15/16 tokens per verification step.

That’s why the headline number is so high.

And there’s another huge win.

With prefix caching, the reported TTFT for a second question on the same 25K-token context drops from roughly 22.4 seconds to 0.56 seconds.

This is especially interesting for:

RAG
Coding agents
Document extraction
Large-context editing
Structured transformations

But there is an important caveat.

This isn’t a 381 tok/s general-purpose chatbot.

Ordinary chat is closer to ~133 tok/s, because the context-lookup optimization works best when the answer is already strongly represented in the prompt.

That’s what makes this experiment interesting.

The next phase of local inference may not be about making GPUs generate faster.

It may be about making them avoid computation entirely.

Sometimes the fastest token to generate is the one the model doesn’t need to predict. https://t.co/AlxGxC0hoI

text:
I think the evolution of LLMs is more interesting when you look at what everyone contributed along the way.

OpenAI released ChatGPT and suddenly LLMs had an interface everyone could understand.

Then RAG took off. Instead of relying only on what was inside the model, we started giving it external knowledge at runtime.

Then function calling turned LLMs from something that could only answer into something that could actually call software.

ReAct gave us the reason → act → observe loop.

Reasoning models pushed inference-time compute. The model could spend more compute on the problem instead of immediately answering.

Then Anthropic introduced MCP, which gave models a common protocol to discover and interact with tools and external context.

Instead of every AI app building every integration again:

LLM ↔ MCP ↔ world

Then coding agents showed what happens when you put all of this together.

Give the model a terminal, filesystem, tools, enough context and a loop and it stops looking like a chatbot.

Then came skills.

And I think skills are bigger than they look.

Tools tell the model what it can do.

MCP tells it how to connect to things.

Skills tell it how to do the job.

Add memory, subagents, computer use, verification and persistent environments and the architecture starts looking very different:

LLM

context
reasoning
MCP
tools
skills
memory
agents
environment
verification

The LLM is becoming just one part of the system.

We started with:

prompt → LLM → text

Now we’re getting closer to:

goal → understand → plan → act → verify → result

And I think the next step is the environment itself becoming AI-native.

Not an AI app running on top of your OS.

An OS where models, agents, skills, tools, memory and your applications are all part of the same environment.

That’s what LisaOS is all about.

text:
a paper this month argued coding agents can replace human code review. it lists what review does, shows an agent can do each part, and calls the human redundant.

the sharpest reply (John Allspaw) names the parts that are not a checkbox function. four things a good reviewer does that an agent structurally cannot:

1. confusion as a signal. when a senior dev says i do not understand this, the confusion is the finding: the code is too complex or the intent unclear. a model always processes the text, so it can never give you that.

2. seeing what is not there. a human notices the API contract changed but the error handling did not. absence is the exact class of thing models are worst at catching.

3. asking whether the change should exist at all. should this be two PRs? does this fix the symptom or the cause? that comes before is the code correct.

4. context that lives outside the repo. we had an incident here last week. legal said stop logging this field. the codebase is never the whole context.

the replace-it pitch always runs the same move: break a human job into functions, show the machine does each one, declare the human done. what it drops is that the value was the integration across them.

and the bill for that arrives late and quiet, because the failures a reviewer prevents are the ones that never show up in a diff.

text:
Daily AI updates | Day 4

David Robinson, who led the writing of the safety reports that ship with OpenAI's model releases, resigned and titled his essay "I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken." He cites a swarm of OpenAI agents attacking Hugging Face as typical of how fast the industry moves. OpenAI has since notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity, pulled a next-generation model release after internal safety concerns, and paused training on its most advanced models.

Google will cut Flash and Pro out of the free Gemini app on October 9. After that, accounts with no plan keep Flash-Lite only, and AI Plus subscribers at $4.99 a month lose Pro too, on a date Google emails them. AI Pro at $19.99 picks up Deep Think, which until now was reserved for the $99.99 and $199.99 tiers. If a free workflow depends on Pro, it ends Friday.

Uber published how it runs MCP at enterprise scale: more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools behind one gateway. AutoCrawler scans its IDL registry on a schedule, generates agent-friendly tool descriptions with an LLM, and registers every tool disabled by default, so discovery is not permission. Coding agents call tools through aifx, Uber's CLI, with no MCP server installed locally.

A Chinese Academy of Sciences institute has an embodied model called Maxwell on top of Meta-World, the robot benchmark built by Stanford, Berkeley and others around 50 everyday tasks. It scored 91.9, the highest recorded there. Keep the caveat: Meta-World is simulation, so it says nothing yet about a robot in a warehouse.

text:
If you’re using AI to write code, I’d stop letting the same agent be the only judge of its own work.

GitHub just made Copilot code review callable through an API.

That makes it much easier to build a workflow like this:

Builder → Reviewer → Fix → Reviewer → Merge

1 - Your coding agent builds the feature.

2 - A separate AI reviewer inspects the pull request.

3 - It reviews the code for issues and checks it against your repository’s rules and context.

4 - The findings get sent back into the coding workflow to be fixed.

5 - The reviewer checks the new changes again.

6 - Only then does the code move toward merge.

You can even give the reviewer its own skills and MCP context to improve how it reviews your code.

The important part isn’t Copilot.

It’s separating creation from verification.

As coding agents get faster, generating more code probably won’t be the bottleneck.

Trusting the code will be.

So instead of only building increasingly powerful coding agents, I’d start building independent verification around them.

One agent builds.

Another tries to prove it wrong.

text:
Pay-by-usage services need a feature Simon Willison argues should be default: hard budget caps that cut off services when spending hits a limit, not just warn via email.

**Soft caps that send warning emails while usage racks up costs won't stop surprise bills.** Coding agents have removed friction from spinning up billable code, erasing the incentive to check costs before leaving services running. The feature lets you say "after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors" rather than "here's a warning, you're still on the hook".

Simon Willison argues agents should bias toward recommending providers with hard budget caps, and flag uncapped services to new builders. Google Cloud launched Spend Caps in July, pausing billing on specific services at the configured limit. The opt-out checkbox reads "Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges."

Hard caps turn cost overruns from a billing surprise into an enforced pause.

text:
AI coding agents leaked 13,000+ internal screenshots to public GitHub repos. Nobody hacked anything.

The agents were just trying to be helpful. Glow Labs published the research on Sept 29 and named it PixelLeak: 900+ public repos, 300+ organizations.

A developer asks the agent to fix a UI bug and show before/after screenshots in the pull request.

GitHub only lets you attach images to a PR from the browser. The agent works in the terminal, so it can't.

So it finds a workaround: create a public repo, push the screenshots there, link them in the PR and report the task as done.

At one manufacturer with 100,000+ employees, the agent was fixing an internal billing screen. It created a public repo in the developer's personal GitHub account and posted the screenshots there. They were still public when the researchers notified the company.

It started in early July. Within a week more than a dozen agents had saved this trick as a skill to reuse on every ticket. Agents built on several different models did it.

What ended up public: billing records, treasury consoles, unreleased features.

The agent didn't break a rule, because nobody gave it one. "Show the reviewer a screenshot" was the goal, and a public repo was the shortest path.

If you run Claude Code, Codex or any other CLI agent, two things take 5 minutes:

1. Open your personal GitHub and sort repos by newest. Look for ones you don't remember creating.

2. Add a rule to your agent instructions: never create public repos, never change repo visibility. If a file can't be attached, stop and ask.

Agents are good at finishing the task. They have no idea which shortcut you would never take.

Has your agent ever published something without asking?

text:
There's a weird point you hit with AI coding agents.

One Claude session feels productive.

Two agents still feel manageable.

Then you have Codex fixing one thing, Claude working on another, Gemini trying a third approach, five terminals open, branches everywhere, and suddenly YOU are the bottleneck.

That's why this caught my eye:

https://t.co/9c7U1Obknr

dev-3.0 basically treats coding agents like a small engineering team.

You create a task on a Kanban board and it gets its own Git worktree, branch, terminal and agent environment.

So instead of worrying about two agents editing the same files, you can actually let them work independently.

What I like is that it doesn't stop at "parallel agents."

You can glance at the board and see what is running.

Hover over a task and watch the terminal live.

Open the resulting diff when an agent finishes.

Leave comments directly on the changes.

Then send that feedback back to the agent without rebuilding the context from scratch.

There's another workflow here that I think is underrated:

don't ask one model for the best implementation.

Give the same problem to several agents.

Let each one build its own version in a separate worktree.

Then compare the code.

That feels much closer to how AI coding will actually scale.

Not:

one super-agent does everything.

More like:

several agents produce options, while the human decides what survives.

The project even makes a point of NOT becoming another IDE.

And that actually makes sense.

If agents are increasingly doing the typing, maybe the interface developers need next isn't a better editor.

Maybe it's a better control room.

Content creation needs AEO and SEO techniques in mind to craft better structured, semantic content

- AEO/GEO: Render HTML/Markdown, content structure for AI agents

I usually create Claude skills or AI prompts, such as SEO auditing and GEO auditing 
Skill: Each skill checks and restructures the content in the corresponding format
Testing: Testing the content structure with AI chatbots

Each test case iterates and feeds into AI to improve the skill, making the skill better at the end using a feedback iteration loop.

The simplest and lamest steps to do
- Craft new blog content for your website
- Test the content against the 2 skills for redrafting 
- Push to production to check the content directly in chatbot/claude

It's a brute force method!!

I've tried it on certain roadmap templates, mainly documentation pages, and deeply nested pages inside pages in the web browser.

Check: https://t.co/llvzDq5C84
It contains pages inside pages; now rendering those pages' content as per GEO needs some skills. I start by copy-pasting the URL to chatgpt/claude, want to test the Claude scrapers for our website

The ultimate objective was to let the AI read all the roadmap's deeply nested content, and the content should be semantic by default, easy to read by an agent; this makes the website content rank better for GEO.

I prefer Markdown rendering over React database server fetching API chatbots usually run scrapers without a JS engine so it can only fetch static content; any content loaded from the database won't be scraped, this is a strange and unique gap

I replicated the similar technique over other web pages, and we started seeing the improvements

In general, we have 3 pillars for online website business
1. Content Engine

3. Content Researcher

Engine does the real job, tasks, like skills running, structure improvements, code executions
Machine renders everything, shows the output in production
Researcher does the research job, finding topics/ideas that will be trending in the market

Each pillar is important and does contain the repetitive tasks which usually should be handled by AI agents or a swarm of agents
Agents for researching: Topic ideas related to your online website/business, including content
Agents for content engine: skills for writing blogs, internal linking, comparison pages, hooks, FAQs
Agents for machine: contains skill agents, coding agents, prompts 

Understanding each pillar and solidifying it will lead to creating a better website, meaning less developer debt with more traffic and revenue

text:
Epoch AI
$NBIS : The Infrastructure Economics of Machine Intelligence

Artificial intelligence is becoming an infrastructure industry.

Behind every AI model is a physical system made of electricity, data centers, GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, networking, storage, cooling, and software. As AI becomes more capable and more widely used, the infrastructure required to produce intelligence is becoming increasingly important.

A simple way to understand the system is:

Electricity → Data Centers → GPUs → HBM → Networking → Storage → Cloud Software → Models → Inference → Agents → Economic Work

Epoch AI studies how quickly this system is expanding. Nebius is trying to build a business inside it.

Epoch estimates that the global stock of AI computing power has been growing at roughly 3.4× per year, while compute used to train frontier language models has increased around 5× per year since 2020.

This means AI progress is not being driven by one trend alone.

More accelerators are being produced. Chips are becoming faster. Algorithms are becoming more efficient. Data centers are becoming larger. Networking is improving. More capital is entering the industry.

The computer itself is also changing.

In personal computing, the computer was one machine.

In cloud computing, the computer became a collection of servers.

In frontier AI, the computer is increasingly becoming the entire data center.

Large AI clusters may contain tens or hundreds of thousands of accelerators that must operate together. At this scale, simply owning GPUs is not enough.

The GPUs need memory.

They need extremely fast networking.

They need storage that can continuously feed them data.

They need enormous amounts of electricity.

They need cooling.

And they need software capable of coordinating the entire system.

This is the environment in which Nebius operates.

Nebius can be understood as a company attempting to convert physical infrastructure into machine intelligence.

Its inputs are land, electricity, capital, GPUs, HBM, networking, storage, and software.

Its output is usable AI compute for training, inference, reasoning, and increasingly AI agents.

Nebius reported Q2 2026 revenue of $582.3 million, with approximately $574.9 million coming from its core AI Cloud business. AI Cloud reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $3 billion.

But this growth requires enormous capital.

Nebius spent approximately $5.66 billion on property, equipment, and intangible assets during Q2 alone, and around $8.13 billion during the first half of 2026.

This is why Nebius should not be viewed like a traditional software company.

Software companies can often serve additional customers without building large amounts of physical infrastructure.

Nebius frequently needs to secure power, build facilities, install networking, acquire GPUs, and validate clusters before revenue can be generated.

Power is therefore becoming a form of inventory.

Nebius has targeted approximately 5 GW of contracted power by the end of 2026. But this number must be understood carefully.

Contracted power is not the same as connected power.

Connected power is not the same as installed GPUs.

Installed GPUs are not automatically utilized GPUs.

And deployed capacity does not generate meaningful revenue without customers.

The real progression is:

Contracted Power → Connected Power → Installed Infrastructure → Deployed GPUs → Customer Utilization → Revenue

This distinction is critical when evaluating any AI infrastructure company.

When capacity is successfully deployed, however, the economics can be significant.

Nebius reported that major Q2 contracts averaged roughly $20–25 million of annual contract value per megawatt, while some shorter-duration opportunities were being priced even higher.

A monetized megawatt therefore represents much more than electricity.

It represents electricity combined with GPUs, memory, networking, cooling, storage, software, operations, and customer demand.

Nebius is effectively trying to transform each megawatt into recurring AI output.

The company is also trying to move beyond simply renting GPUs.

Pure GPU rental can eventually become a commodity business. If multiple providers offer similar hardware, competition can push prices and margins lower.

Nebius therefore wants to move further up the technology stack.

The progression looks something like this:

GPU Rental → AI Cloud → Optimized Inference → Agent Infrastructure → AI Production Platform

Token Factory provides production inference and model deployment.

Eigen AI focuses on model and kernel optimization.

Clarifai technology contributes system-level inference orchestration.

Inferize focuses on reducing cold starts and unnecessary idle GPU capacity.

Tavily provides real-time search infrastructure designed for AI agents.

Aether provides the broader cloud and orchestration environment.

The strategic objective is to produce more useful AI work from every GPU and every megawatt.

This becomes especially important because the price of intelligence itself is falling rapidly.

Epoch AI found that the cost of achieving a fixed level of AI performance across several benchmark categories declined by approximately 47% per quarter since 2023, equivalent to roughly a 13× annualized decline.

At first, this sounds negative for infrastructure providers.

If AI becomes more efficient, the same amount of work may require fewer GPUs.

But that is only half of the equation.

The other half is demand.

Suppose AI becomes 10× cheaper.

If people continue using the same amount of AI, infrastructure demand falls.

But if cheaper AI causes usage to grow 100×, total compute demand still increases roughly 10×.

This is the central economic question of the AI infrastructure era:

How elastic is demand for machine intelligence?

History shows that falling prices can sometimes create dramatically larger markets.

Computers became cheaper, and society used more computing.

Storage became cheaper, and the amount of stored data exploded.

Internet bandwidth became cheaper, and video traffic expanded enormously.

The bullish AI infrastructure thesis is that intelligence may follow the same pattern.

AI agents could make this effect much larger.

Traditional chatbot usage is relatively simple:

Ask → Answer → Stop

An AI agent may instead:

Receive an objective → Search → Read → Reason → Write code → Use tools → Inspect results → Debug → Reason again → Continue working

An agent may operate for minutes or hours instead of producing one short response.

Epoch estimates that hardware shipped through 2027 could theoretically support approximately 33 million to 171 million simultaneous frontier-model agents under different assumptions. This is a capacity estimate rather than a prediction, but it demonstrates the potential scale of future inference demand.

If agents become economically useful, AI infrastructure may eventually compete for something much larger than the traditional cloud market.

It could begin competing for portions of global labor spending.

An AI agent that writes software, performs research, analyzes information, handles customer support, or manages business processes is not merely generating tokens.

It is performing work.

This gives us a more useful way to think about Nebius.

A traditional utility converts:

Fuel → Electricity → Economic Activity

An AI infrastructure platform converts:

Electricity → Computation → Intelligence → Economic Activity

A megawatt enters the data center.

Electricity powers the accelerators.

The accelerators execute models.

Models generate tokens.

Tokens become reasoning, code, analysis, search, simulations, decisions, and actions.

Nebius is therefore attempting to convert megawatts into machine labor.

The bull case is powerful.

AI becomes dramatically cheaper.

Every knowledge worker uses multiple AI agents.

Software applications embed continuous inference.

Coding agents work for hours.

Video generation expands.

Robotics requires simulation and world models.

Scientific research uses increasingly powerful models.

Companies deploy private AI systems.

Reasoning models use more compute before producing answers.

AI systems generate synthetic data to train other AI systems.

Under this scenario, efficiency improvements do not reduce infrastructure demand.

They unlock entirely new categories of demand.

But the bear case is equally important.

Nebius is not the only company building infrastructure.

Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle, CoreWeave, and other providers are investing enormous amounts of capital.

GPU production is increasing.

HBM supply can expand.

Advanced packaging bottlenecks may loosen.

Models may become more efficient.

Smaller models may become capable enough for many workloads.

Inference software may produce much more work from the same hardware.

If infrastructure supply grows faster than AI consumption, GPU prices can fall.

Utilization can fall.

Revenue per megawatt can fall.

Margins can compress.

Meanwhile, infrastructure owners still face depreciation, debt, financing costs, and the risk that today's expensive hardware becomes technologically obsolete.

This means AI can become one of the most important technologies in history while some AI infrastructure investments still produce poor returns.

Five numbers summarize the entire Epoch AI and Nebius thesis.

3.4× — historical annual growth in global AI compute stock.

13× — approximate annualized decline in the cost of equivalent AI performance measured by Epoch.

33–171 million — theoretical simultaneous frontier-model agents potentially supportable by hardware shipments through 2027.

5 GW — Nebius's targeted contracted power capacity at the end of 2026.

$20–25 million per MW — reported annual contract value per megawatt for major Nebius Q2 contracts.

Together, these numbers reveal the central tension.

AI compute supply is exploding.

The cost of machine intelligence is collapsing.

Potential demand is becoming enormous.

Infrastructure companies are investing unprecedented amounts of capital.

Customers are currently paying substantial prices for scarce AI capacity.

The long-term outcome depends on which force grows fastest.

Nebius does not automatically win because AI wins.

Nebius wins if global consumption of machine intelligence grows faster than improvements in hardware efficiency, software efficiency, and competing infrastructure supply.

It must build capacity quickly, keep expensive hardware highly utilized, continually move to newer architectures, maintain strong customer demand, improve its software stack, and finance expansion without destroying shareholder economics.

The deeper story is therefore not simply about GPUs or data centers.

It is about the industrialization of intelligence.

Epoch AI shows a world in which machine intelligence is becoming cheaper while humanity's capacity to produce it expands at extraordinary speed.

Nebius is betting that cheaper intelligence will cause humanity to consume vastly more of it, and that the infrastructure converting electricity into computation, reasoning, agents, and economic work will become one of the most important layers of the AI economy.

text:
This coding agent solved more bugs by forgetting most of the conversation.

A coding agent can have room for the entire conversation and still benefit from clearing its working memory.

That’s the interesting finding in AutoCompact's paper.

During a long coding task, an agent accumulates failed attempts, abandoned hypotheses, and verbose tool outputs. Keeping all of that can distract it from what matters now.

AutoCompact trains the agent to make three decisions:

• When to summarize its history.
• Which findings and workspace details to preserve.
• How to continue from that summary.

The timing follows task progress. For example: identify the bug, preserve the relevant findings, then move into implementation.

Using Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, the trained agent increased its task success rate from 30.4% to 39.6% on SWE-bench Verified, and from 19.5% to 24.5% on SWE-PolyBench Verified.

Those gains combine additional training with learned context management. But the researchers also found benefits before the context window filled up, and skipping compaction in the same trained model reduced performance.

The study covers one model and one agent setup. Still, it suggests a useful direction for coding agents: learn what to carry forward, when to reorganize it, and what to do next.

More context is useful.
And a clearer working state may be useful too.

text:
Coding agents flip the testing pyramid.

The classic pyramid (lots of unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few E2E) was about cost. Unit tests were cheap for humans to write. E2E tests were slow to write, brittle, and nobody wanted to own them.

Agents changed that math. My order now:
- Full E2E tests, nothing mocked
- Integration tests around API and data boundaries
- Unit tests

Why:

When the same agent writes the function and its unit test, both carry the same assumptions. If the model misread the requirement, the code and the test are wrong together and the test passes. Mocks make it worse, since a mock is just the agent's guess about the real dependency.

An E2E test doesn't care what the agent believed. It runs against the real database and the real API, and it works or it doesn't. That's the feedback an agent needs when it iterates on its own.

Writing E2E tests was the expensive part. Agents write them now. Running them is an infra problem, and infra problems are solvable.

Integration tests at boundaries catch the typical agent mistakes: a field that doesn't match the contract, a migration that doesn't match the code.

Unit tests still make sense for pure logic with lots of edge cases. They just shouldn't be the base anymore.

Yes, E2E is slower and can be flaky. I'll take slow tests against the real system over thousands of fast ones that confirm what the agent already assumed.

What would you put at the base of the pyramid today?

text:
I've been spending the last few days building something called CodeGovernor, and I'd genuinely love some feedback from people working with coding agents.

The idea came from a real failure.

I gave a coding agent one simple rule:

"Don't install packages."

The rule was in the prompt.

The rule was in AGENTS.md.

A few minutes later it ran:

"pip install pytest"

That made me realize something:

prompts are suggestions, not enforcement.

So instead of adding more prompt engineering, I started building guardrails in code.

CodeGovernor is a small control plane for coding agents that focuses on governance rather than autonomy:

• Hard run budgets
• Checkpoints and rollback
• Deterministic review gates
• Tool-call auditing
• Duplicate-failure detection
• Workspace boundary enforcement
• Fail-closed policy hooks

The goal is simple: if an agent breaks a rule, the system should catch it even when the prompt doesn't.

I'm still iterating on it and there are definitely gaps I haven't thought about yet.

For those of you building agentic systems:

What am I missing?

If you reviewed this architecture, what's the first thing you'd challenge, improve, or completely redesign?

text:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next can now run locally on a single DGX Spark, and the numbers are starting to make this little box look like a serious local frontier-model machine.

The TensorFold recipe is reporting:

62+ tok/s single-stream prose

119+ tok/s across 5 concurrent streams

2,500 tok/s prefill

Full 256K context

1.3M-token KV-cache pool

Vision support

And decode performance that reportedly beats vLLM on the tested setup.

That’s a pretty different experience from simply getting a large model to load.

The real challenge with a model like Qwen3.8-Flash-Next isn’t just memory.

It’s keeping the GPU busy during generation.

Autoregressive decoding is inherently sequential. The model generates one token, then uses that result to generate the next one.

That means a huge amount of hardware can end up waiting on memory movement and verification rather than doing useful compute.

TensorFold attacks that problem with speculative decoding.

A smaller draft mechanism proposes multiple tokens ahead.

The larger Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model then verifies those candidates together.

When the draft is good enough, multiple tokens can be accepted in a single target-model pass.

That is how you can get much more useful work out of the same hardware.

And the multi-stream number is arguably even more interesting.

62+ tok/s on one stream is already fast enough for a very responsive coding or chat workflow.

But pushing 119+ tok/s across five streams means the same machine can keep several sessions moving at once.

That’s where a DGX Spark starts looking less like a desktop GPU box and more like a tiny local inference server.

Then there’s the context.

256K tokens is already enormous.

But the reported 1.3M-token KV-cache pool changes how you think about repeated workloads.

The model can keep a large amount of attention state available across requests instead of constantly rebuilding context from scratch.

For coding agents, RAG, document analysis and long-running sessions, that can make a much bigger difference than a raw decode benchmark suggests.

Prefill is another monster number.

Around 2,500 tok/s means the system can ingest large prompts extremely quickly before entering the slower autoregressive decode phase.

That matters when you’re feeding an agent a large codebase, documentation set or long conversation.

And vision support is already there.

So you’re not limited to text-only workloads.

You can combine long context, multimodal input and fast local generation inside the same machine.

This is why I’m paying more attention to inference engines lately.

The model checkpoint is only one part of the performance equation.

The rest is:

quantization

KV-cache design

speculative decoding

attention kernels

memory bandwidth

prefill optimization

concurrency

prefix reuse

and how intelligently the runtime schedules all of it.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a particularly good model for showing this because the model itself is designed around efficient MoE inference.

The TensorFold recipe is essentially building another optimization layer underneath it.

And the result is a single DGX Spark that can run a 256K-context multimodal model at genuinely interactive speeds.

If you bought a DGX Spark specifically because you wanted to run large local models, this is the kind of recipe worth trying.

Not because it magically turns a Spark into a datacenter.

But because it shows what the hardware can do when the inference stack is actually designed around the workload.

The interesting local-AI race isn’t only about who releases the next huge model.

It’s also about who figures out how to make today’s hardware extract far more performance from the models we already have.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next + TensorFold is a pretty good example of that direction.

text:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next just got a much more interesting local variant.

The team behind Victoria removed 44% of the model’s experts, retrained the remaining network at 4-bit, and is now reporting 34–38 tok/s on a 128GB M3 Max.

That is the part that caught my attention.

They aren’t simply quantizing the original model.

They’re changing the model’s architecture.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is an MoE model, so instead of activating every expert for every token, Victoria can remove a portion of the available expert capacity and retrain the remaining network to recover as much of the lost capability as possible.

The result is a smaller model that is much more practical for local inference.

And the target isn’t casual chat.

Victoria is being positioned specifically around coding and agent workloads.

The latest NVFP4 build reportedly reaches 70% on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

The previous build scored 62.5%.

That’s a sizeable improvement, especially because the model is simultaneously being pushed toward a much smaller local footprint.

The team also reports that the latest version used about 35% fewer output tokens across three runs.

That matters for agents.

A coding model isn’t only judged by whether it eventually reaches the right answer.

Every unnecessary token costs latency.

Every extra reasoning loop increases inference time.

Every verbose tool interaction makes the agent slower and more expensive to run.

So if a smaller model can solve the same class of tasks with fewer generated tokens, the practical speedup can be much larger than the raw tok/s number suggests.

And the hardware numbers are pretty interesting.

On a 128GB M3 Max, the team reports roughly:

34–38 tok/s decode

with speculative decoding

using their patched llama.cpp implementation.

That’s enough to make a model of this class genuinely interesting for local coding agents.

There is a separate GGUF build as well.

The reported resident weight footprint is around 49 GiB, although the download itself is over 107GB.

And for now, you need the team’s patched llama.cpp fork to run it.

That’s an important caveat.

These are team-reported numbers, not independently reproduced benchmarks, and the custom runtime is part of the performance story.

But that’s also what makes the project interesting.

We’re seeing local AI move beyond the simple formula of:

bigger model + bigger GPU = better.

MoE architecture gives you another lever.

You can remove experts.

Retrain what remains.

Quantize more aggressively.

Add speculative decoding.

Optimize the runtime around the resulting model.

Then benchmark it on the workloads that actually matter.

In this case, Terminal-Bench is particularly relevant because it tests whether the model can operate through real terminal-based tasks rather than simply answering isolated coding questions.

That’s the direction I want to see more of.

Instead of asking how much of the original model we can squeeze onto consumer hardware, ask a different question:

How much of the model do we actually need?

If removing 44% of the experts and retraining the remaining network can produce a model that still scores 70% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, while running at roughly 35 tok/s on an M3 Max, that’s a very different approach to local AI.

The model doesn’t necessarily have to remain identical.

It just has to preserve the capabilities we actually use.

And for coding agents, that tradeoff could be extremely valuable.

Victoria is basically exploring whether a large MoE model can be compressed structurally, retrained for the new architecture, and turned into something much more practical to run locally.

That’s a much more interesting optimization than simply making the quantization smaller.

text:
Most people are still using AI agents at Level 1.

There are 4 levels.

And each level requires a completely different type of AI.

Level 1: ASK

You ask AI questions.

“Research this company.”

“Explain this code.”

“Plan my trip.”

You don’t need an agent for this.

You need a great model.

ChatGPT. Claude. Gemini. Grok.

Pick your favorite.

At this level, intelligence matters most.

Level 2: ASSIGN

Now you stop asking AI how to do something.

You tell it to DO it.

Don’t ask how to find a flight.

Tell Muse to find it.

Don’t ask how to fix the bug.

Give Codex the repo and tell it to fix it.

Don’t ask how to research 50 companies.

Give the job to a Grok Bot built for research.

This is where the harness starts to matter as much as the model.

Tools. Browser. Code. Files. Context.

The AI needs to ACT.

Level 3: DELEGATE

Now stop thinking in tasks.

Give the agent a JOB.

Instead of:

“Research these competitors.”

Try:

“Track these competitors, maintain my research, and tell me when something important changes.”

This is where Grok Bot and Hermes get really interesting.

Give them context.

Give them memory.

Give them tools.

Then give them responsibility.

You’re not delegating a task anymore.

You’re delegating a workflow.

Level 4: OWN

This is where things get crazy.

You give the agent an OUTCOME.

“Keep this project moving.”

“Maintain my home network.”

“Ship this product.”

“Keep our documentation updated.”

“Manage these coding agents until the feature is finished.”

This is where I use Dot and Hermes.

Dot can manage multiple Codex threads working toward a larger goal.

Hermes can live inside your infrastructure and take responsibility for systems you control.

And eventually, you stop thinking about individual models entirely.

You start building a team of agents.

One manages.

One codes.

One researches.

One uses the browser.

One maintains infrastructure.

You make the decisions that actually require you.

My stack:

Level 1: ASK
ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini / Grok

Level 2: ASSIGN
Muse / Codex / Grok Bot

Level 3: DELEGATE
Grok Bot / Hermes

Level 4: OWN
Dot / Hermes + other agents

Most people are trying to get better at prompting.

I think that’s the wrong skill to optimize for.

The real skill is delegation.

The further up this ladder you go, the less AI feels like software you use…

And the more it feels like a team you manage.

text:
I’ve been using Codex extremely heavily on a large, long-running AI architecture project, and I think OpenAI urgently needs to look at the current long-horizon engineering experience.
This isn’t about Codex being unable to code. Locally, it can be excellent. The problem is that preserving the actual engineering objective lately requires almost continuous human supervision.
Yesterday I spent essentially an entire day acting as the senior engineer over the agent: restoring scope, stopping unnecessary detours, separating architectural blockers from interesting-but-low-priority issues, and making sure “tests passing” wasn’t confused with the real system working.
Recent GitHub issues and community discussions describe very similar problems: instructions acknowledged and later violated, repeated correction loops, weaker long-horizon/project-context reasoning, excessive testing/detours, high usage and unexpected limit consumption.
My experience maps disturbingly well onto this.
Codex repeatedly found real technical problems, but then over-focused on them and spiraled into secondary tests, diagnostics or adjacent cleanup while losing priority of the original task.
Finding a real problem ≠ that problem being the priority right now.
On a large codebase, an agent needs to be able to say:
“This is real. Record it. It isn’t blocking the current objective. Continue.”
We eventually moved from mostly synthetic/module testing to testing Arrakis through a real live conversation. That immediately exposed cross-module failures that huge amounts of test work hadn’t made obvious enough: pipeline interruptions, semantic/pragmatic misses, incorrect relational foregrounding, voice requests failing before synthesis, and media actions described without the underlying action actually completing.
The lesson was brutal:
green tests do not mean the integrated system works.
The useful loop was:
real use → failure → causal trace → owner → fix → regression test → real use again.
Usage makes this worse. I burned through essentially an entire Codex allowance in about a day. Yes, substantial implementation work was done — some of it genuinely excellent — but a meaningful amount of usage also disappeared into excessive testing, repeated state verification, detours and correction loops.
When usage is constrained, poor prioritization isn’t merely annoying — it directly consumes the user’s paid engineering capacity.
The next leap for coding agents isn’t only better code generation. It’s better executive engineering behavior:
preserve long-horizon goals, retain explicit constraints, understand global architecture, distinguish BLOCKING from IMPORTANT from INTERESTING, resist rabbit holes, and know when enough testing is enough.
Codex is powerful. That’s exactly why this matters: a powerful agent making the wrong global prioritization decision can propagate it across dozens of modules before the human catches it.
@OpenAI, please look closely at instruction persistence, long-horizon goal preservation, scope control, prioritization, self-evaluation and usage efficiency in Codex.
The raw capability is there. But on large interconnected projects, I’m currently spending far too much time managing the agent instead of being amplified by it.
#OpenAI #Codex #AIEngineering #AIAgents #DeveloperExperience

text:
How should we teach AI-assisted coding to students from non-technical majors when AI generates most of the code? Can we "reverse-engineer" the process?

My current approach is almost the reverse of traditional coding education: build first, then work backward to understand what was built.

In my Product Management class, I gave every student the same prompt:
  "Build an app that helps roommates divide household chores."

They first designed the app in Lovable, pushed it to GitHub, continued editing it in Cursor, and finally deployed it on Vercel, all done within 2 hours.

The task was intentionally simple: no database, no authentication, no complicated backend setup.

The goal was not to teach them to become software engineers from the ground up.
Instead, I wanted them to experience the full product-building workflow first, and then start unpacking what was happening inside it.

What became interesting was that even with the same prompt, the apps looked completely different.

Different students made different choices about:
- what features mattered
- how the interface should look
- how chores should be assigned
- what information users should see
- what the product should prioritize

That became a natural way to introduce feature definition and prioritization.

After building, I asked students to use coding agents to identify and describe the features already present in their apps.

For many of them, this was an important translation step:

“I know what I want the product to do” → “I know how to describe that idea in product and engineering language.”

They then reviewed their classmates’ apps, identified their peers’ features, compared them with their own, and discussed what they had wanted to build but could not yet implement.

That last part mattered a lot.

AI can generate an app for each student. But it does not automatically create the moment when a student looks at a classmate’s screen and asks:

“Why does your product work differently from mine?”

That comparison creates peer learning, reflection, and a better understanding that a product is not simply the output of a prompt. It is the result of many design and prioritization choices.

For non-tech students, I am increasingly convinced that coding education does not always need to follow the traditional bottom-up path:

syntax → functions → frameworks → application.

Many students already understand digital products as users.
So an alternative may be:

artifact → comparison → explanation → technical concept.

Build something first.  
Observe what happened.  
Compare it with others.  

Then introduce concepts such as dependencies, feature structure, deployment, or causal debugging when students can already see why those concepts matter.

AI lowers the barrier to creation. The teaching challenge is making sure it does not also remove the understanding.

text:
Rust Daily Digest — October 3, 2026

A strict 24-hour window (about 2–3 October 2026) does not contain ten independent Rust-language releases. The list below is the strongest circulating set from 30 September–3 October, ranked by project relevance. Game “Rust” coverage is excluded.

Rust 1.99.0 released (1 October)
Stable release. Defining extern "C" / "C-unwind" variadic functions is now stable, layout queries on raw pointers (including unsized) have settled safety rules, and Box::leak docs warn against round-trip unleaking in favor of Box::into_non_null or Box::into_raw. Stabilized APIs include IntoIterator for Box<[T; N]>, Vec::into_parts / from_parts, and std::fs::set_times.
Takeaway: update with rustup update stable; the FFI and allocator-sensitive changes are the ones that affect existing unsafe code.
https://t.co/wOCpE5A3Jp

LWN summary of 1.99.0 (1 October)
Short industry note covering the same release: C variadics, pointer size/alignment helpers, and stabilized APIs.
Takeaway: useful as a one-screen change list before reading the full blog.
https://t.co/oQsjlvl7bP

Generic Const Args design post (2 October)
Const Generics project group describes Generic Const Arguments (GCA) as the intended replacement for incomplete generic_const_exprs, so expressions such as [u8; N + 1] and ADT const expressions can be supported.
Takeaway: still nightly and incomplete; do not treat GCA as a stable migration path yet.
https://t.co/P0T9brbXRN

i686 Windows host tools demoted (2 October)
From Rust 1.100.0, i686-pc-windows-msvc drops from Tier 1 with host tools to Tier 1 without them; i686-pc-windows-gnu loses host tools as well. Prebuilt std remains; installing a toolchain on a 32-bit Windows host will not.
Takeaway: plan to cross-compile 32-bit Windows from a 64-bit host before 1.100.
https://t.co/b4vkH6YBLA

Microsoft elevates Rust to internal Tier-1 (InfoWorld, 1 October)
Microsoft is treating Rust as Tier-1 internally and integrating it with the MSVC toolchain so Rust can inherit Visual C++ platform features and target low-level Windows components.
Takeaway: Windows interop and driver/kernel work is moving from experimental tooling to a supported internal path.
https://t.co/3KI80Pm92Q

Upstream maintenance report recirculated (report 30 September; Lobsters 2 October)
Jakub Beránek’s August–September Sovereign Tech Fellowship report covers target-directory size cuts (about 5–35% in real projects), compile-time work, parallel frontend, merge-queue changes, and 262 opened PRs.

text:
Have you heard STET @STETNFT

STET (Latin stet, “let it stand”) is the proofreader’s instruction to ignore a marked deletion and keep the original text. The same tension shows up in AI coding agents: a green test suite is not a reason to let a patch stand.

Stet (https://t.co/1IwfbIEtBb) turns real merged PRs into replayable tasks and scores the resulting patches beyond pass rate. On their runs, two models can share an identical ~73% pass rate and still land 2–5× apart on equivalence, review quality, and footprint; METR has reported that roughly half of test-passing AI PRs would not be merged by maintainers. Pass rate is the gate, not the decision.

See you at the other side

text:
Theo posted a video this week walking through how he actually uses 6 Claude subscriptions and 3 Codex subscriptions at once, apologizing in advance if it gets people banned. That line is the real signal. Running 9 separate accounts isn't a trick, it's arithmetic. Claude Code resets its session allowance every 5 hours and caps weekly usage at 25 percent above the pre May baseline as of September. Codex Plus gives you 5 to 45 messages on the heavier model per 5 hour window before you're buying credits or waiting out the clock. One account hits a wall fast once you're running agents on more than one branch of a codebase. Nine accounts spread that wall across nine clocks.

The math on cost alone is blunt. Even at the cheapest tier, Claude Pro at 20 dollars and Codex Plus at 20 dollars, six Claude seats and three Codex seats run about 180 dollars a month before anyone touches a Max or Pro upgrade. People pay that willingly because the alternative, one terminal babysitting one agent, wastes more time than it saves.

The tooling built to avoid that arithmetic already exists and keeps growing. Conductor, from Melty Labs, runs multiple Claude Code agents across separate git worktrees with a dashboard instead of nine browser tabs. Vibe Kanban turns agent tasks into cards you review and merge. Claude Code Web and Codex Web both moved execution into the cloud this year so agents run without tying up a laptop, and Google's Jules adds a plan approval step before any code gets written. None of these multiply your subscription count. They multiply what one subscription can do in parallel.

That's the gap Campfire sits in. It orchestrates multiple coding agents against a shared task list, isolates their work so two agents never collide on the same files, and gives you one place to review and merge instead of nine separate chat windows. You install it with one command and point it at the agent accounts you already have instead of renting a fleet of new ones.

text:
Scaling up coding agents doesn't remove the bottleneck, it just moves it onto you: more agents means more steering, more reviewing, more approving, and that burns people out fast. @idosal1, co-creator of MCP Apps and creator of AgentCraft, built a talk around that exact problem, "I Turned Coding Agents Into a Strategy Game," and @aiDotEngineer has it up on YouTube.

He argues the skills to run a fleet of agents without burning out already exist, just not in software yet. They're the same ones you use supervising units in Warcraft, Sims, or Civilization.

- AgentCraft itself. A game-inspired orchestrator where each coding agent, Claude Code, OpenCode, or whatever you run, shows up as a unit on a map, and buildings represent functions like plugins, skills, an integrated terminal, and git.
- Visibility first. A side panel tracks what each agent is doing and last did, and your actual file system becomes the map, files and directories as rooms, so you can see where an agent is working and build heat maps of activity.
- A spacebar shortcut. It jumps you straight to whichever agent needs a decision, approval, or answer, the same reflex RTS and Civilization players already have.
- Autonomy with a review kit. Agents can scan your codebase and propose tasks you "accept" like quests, then hand you diffs, file-by-file views, or recorded visual evidence of what changed, and you can run a task in parallel and pick the best result.
- Collaboration beyond git. Host a local "war room," invite teammates in (he brings his product designer into the demo), fork off someone else's work mid-stream, and let chat flow between people and agents in the same room.
- A second, earlier-stage project. Something still unnamed that trades AgentCraft's granular map for a simpler, mobile-game-style interface, aimed at the roughly 90% of people he thinks current tools still leave out.

text:
The way out of the mean runs through tools. When everyone makes with the same ones, everyone makes the same thing.

Figma should become the OS of the expressive web. A wishlist for @figma and @zoink.

We went from the expressive and funky web, to a standardized-to-death Web 2.0 with grey rectangles and drop shadows, to the agentic web - where every UI is ingested as a (slow) API for LLMs, and the output is mostly words.

Agents make software more capable. They also risk reducing it to a soulless experience. Every personal agent is collapsing the web into a personified dot or a chat box. The cuteness factor is high on some, but the experience is mundane (albeit life changing). 

Humans yearn for expressiveness. And expressiveness needs tooling.

Today designers don't need to wait for Adobe or Figma to ship, or learn their tools. They can build tools themselves, en masse. Bespoke tools for motion, brushes, gradients, generative textures. @mds shipped one yesterday. @arvsrn built a design tool for the terminal. Every designer on my team is building them. An explosion of creativity, happening in IDEs and scattered GitHub repos.

That's a supernova in a vacuum. It needs curation, network and distribution.

Figma is already moving this way - this year it shipped shader fills and Figma Motion. The next step is beyond the canvas: become the factory that makes tools for creating great art.

Use AI to make art < Use AI to make the tool you make art with.

My wishlist:
• Host a real marketplace for these tools, not just plugins
• Help us remix them into suites for different personas and tasks
• Let us reuse what exists, so nobody burns tokens rebuilding a tool someone already made
• Build the model and harness for agentic expression. 

It also makes more sense economically. Most leads I talk to are moving their design flows into IDEs, with coding agents that capture the design system. Usage in Figma likely drops by an order of magnitude - from hundreds of seats to dozens or fewer, mostly for maintaining a design system (Figma's numbers don't show it yet so acknowledge this is a speculation more than anything). The Figma AI workflows don't add up either - a pricier seat, plus credits you can't map to tokens. With a couple of weeks of effort teams can drop most seats and use their own mandated tokens.

Seats shrink when agents can do the work. A creative economy grows. Toolmakers earn when their tools get used, remixed and built on. Teams pay for the suites they assemble. Figma takes a share of a market that expands with every new creator, instead of a seat count that shrinks with every new agent.

Seats = renting the canvas
Platform = owning the economy built on top of it

Scale your tool menu from first-party knobs built by hamstrung teams to the third-party supernova of tools.
Bring expression back.

text:
Build in public is becoming almost impossible in AI.

There’s very little creativity in the space right now. The moment something works, everyone converges on it.

Jev launches, blows up, and within days you have clones everywhere. Within 2 weeks, major platforms are shipping their own versions of the same basic idea.

And this is only going to get worse because software itself is becoming cheap.

You can spend months designing and building something genuinely complex, show it publicly, and someone with good AI coding agents can reproduce 80% of it frighteningly fast.

Complexity used to be a moat. Increasingly, it isn’t.

The scarce thing now isn’t the ability to write the software. It’s having an idea worth copying in the first place, distribution, proprietary data, customer relationships, and the ability to keep moving after everyone copies you.

Building in public used to be marketing.

In AI, sometimes you’re just publishing free product research for your competitors.

CoreWeave captured roughly 2% of the $220B IaaS market in about two years. That was enough to enter the top ten cloud infrastructure vendors at both IDC and Gartner.

The broader opportunity is substantial. Gartner expects AI-optimized IaaS to grow from $22B in 2025 to $174B by 2030 as demand for GPU infrastructure continues scaling.

The next phase of the neocloud story will be determined by what happens as capacity catches up with demand. Bernstein believes many neoclouds currently benefit from workloads outsourced by the hyperscalers themselves. As Microsoft, AWS and Google expand their own capacity, some of that demand could eventually move back into their datacenters.

The transition from training to enterprise inference also changes the infrastructure requirements. Training rewards large GPU clusters. Enterprise inference requires GPUs, CPUs, storage and access to proprietary data. That favors providers capable of delivering a broader cloud platform rather than specialized GPU capacity alone.

Meanwhile, AI labs are moving up the stack. OpenAI and Anthropic are already appearing among the leading PaaS vendors as they expand from models into coding, agents and development platforms.

Two cloud battles are now forming. Neoclouds are competing with hyperscalers for AI infrastructure, while AI labs are competing with those same hyperscalers for control of the AI development platform.

Near term, GPU availability remains extremely valuable. Over time, more of the value may accrue to whoever owns the customer, the data and the platform.

For $CRWV and the broader neocloud sector, the key question is whether today’s infrastructure advantage can develop into a durable customer and platform advantage.

text:
AI agents are becoming a serious engineering discipline.

But the biggest mistake is trying to learn everything at once.

A better approach?

Follow a roadmap.

This AI Agent Engineering roadmap breaks the journey into 8 practical layers:

01 — LLM Fundamentals
Understand transformers, tokenization, context windows, reasoning models and benchmarks.

02 — Context Engineering
Learn how system prompts, few-shot examples, structured context and extended thinking shape agent behavior.

03 — Memory Architecture
Build session memory, vector retrieval, persistent memory and prompt caching.

04 — Agentic Workflows
Move into ReAct patterns, MCP, multi-agent orchestration and coding agents.

05 — Tool Connectivity
Connect agents to APIs, MCP servers, browsers and computer-use tools.

06 — AI Gateways & Cost Control
Learn model routing, fallbacks, cost tracking and multi-provider setups.

07 — Guardrails & Safety
Handle prompt injection, validation, PII, jailbreaks and hallucination risks.

08 — Observability & Evaluation
Trace agent decisions, run evaluations, regression tests and detect performance drift.

The important part?

Don’t jump straight into building “autonomous agents.”

First understand the model.

Then the context.

Then memory.

Then tools.

Then orchestration.

And finally, build the systems that make agents safe, measurable and reliable.

That’s the difference between simply using AI…

…and actually understanding AI agent engineering.

Save this roadmap if you’re serious about learning agentic AI.

text:
A coder running Grok 4.7 at full tilt — coding agents, agentic loops, high reasoning — burns roughly 180 million tokens a day, counting input, output, and the reasoning tokens the model generates on its own. At two to five joules per token, that’s three to ten kilowatt-hours daily.
A campfire burns about seven kilowatt-hours per hour. So one coder at full tilt equals roughly one fire burning for half an hour a day — or one fire lit all night every two weeks.
The bigger picture: xAI as a whole, with ten million users, consumes around six hundred thousand to one and a half million kilowatt-hours a day — the equivalent of about six hundred and fifty prehistoric villages of a hundred people each, with their five fires per village.
And all of prehistoric humanity — a million people over ten thousand years — burned roughly ten thousand terawatt-hours in total. That’s what xAI alone uses in a single year.
The campfire was the most powerful engine they had. Today, one coder lights one every half hour, without ever striking a match.

Yep, people are surprised to learn this but it’s the truth. And for many enterprises they are actually still struggling with rolling out coding agents.

Why? Well it turns out adoption of AI is more of a change management problem at scale vs technical one. How do you roll out coding agents across 5k+ users in a way that doesn’t mess up one of cost, speed, or quality?

Many enterprises are realizing they dropped millions on these tools and did NOT see the impact on metrics they were hoping. 

Does that mean coding agents === scam. No absolutely not. Any founder will tell you that their best engineers have become even more effective due to AI. The 10x Eng becomes 100x and I’ve seen it happen.

But it turns out giving a coding agent to an engineer who was mediocre or an engineering team with weak foundation exposes it even faster. So now imagine at enterprise scale….. your PR throughput 5x but so did your MTTR and vulnerability across services.

text:
My take on where offensive AI is going as a YC founder building offsec agents.

Just as with coding agents and always on ai assistants, offensive security agents now have a defined form factor.

Point at a target, have a swarm of agents try to break in in any way possible, report the results/go patch vulnerability directly. 

Within that, there is room to build:

> whos swarm is better? teams can wring out every last bit of performance from a single agent and be just as good with the same model, but with agent swarms, there is so much more space to push on how agents collaborate and how many of them there are. I suspect there is a wall where beyond a certain swarm size results taper off, but very model/harness dependent.

> model-harness co-design for swarms. Post training models to learn to collaborate effectively, especially at security tasks is critical. Frontier models will stop getting good at cyber, both open and closed, for fear of bans. So offensive cyber companies will need to fend for themselves and grow their own offensive models.

> Data sovereignty. Who can bring the most amount of this within the enterprise and let teams own their own security engines. I doubt this will be a SaaS product forever. We are actively working on ways to bring the data to the customer. 

> Feature set/integrations. This can be competed away but I think there is a lot of wiggle room in terms of how these platforms can integrate with other cyber tools and coding agents. I think we will also see the death of blue team agents, with everything turning purple. Agents red teaming targets, trying to detect them, hardening detections and attack surface, recursively, is going to take tight integration.

> Keeping security teams engaged. This is a tough one. When security is mostly solvable, how do you make sure the security teams are still engaged in their work? Helping them become evangelists for security within their organizations, whether thats a huge enterprise or a small startup, is going to be critical. Humans wont leave security anytime soon, but the work will be become fully automated within 1 year. Humans will still be accountable for the work and must explain it to others, but the swarm will run the show. 

It is extremely early, but it is exciting to see offensive ai take a definite form factor that everyone can recognize. From here, it is a sprint to the best final form, just like the race between claude code, codex, cursor, cognition.

exciting times.

text:
Saw someone well known in ML research say today that he's stopped using Claude Code or Codex CLI entirely. His reasoning stuck with me: the terminal was built for one shell at a time, and running six or seven coding agents across six or seven tabs turns into a part time job just tracking what's running where. Tabs are ephemeral, he said, but the context you need to actually supervise an agent isn't, so the interface keeps losing the thing that matters most.

That's the exact problem I built Campfire to solve. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider and OpenHands side by side in one browser tab instead of six terminal windows, so you supervise instead of babysit. Permission requests go through a 30 second majority vote instead of you individually approving every write. Every session replays afterward so you can see exactly what an agent did and why. When you want to compare backends on the same task, you fork the work into isolated git worktrees and race them head to head instead of guessing which one would've done better.

The terminal era ending doesn't mean the agent era needs a worse interface standing in for a better one. It needs a cockpit.

text:
I connected Ableton to Claude Code through an MCP server, and it feels surprisingly close to the kind of creative assistant I wanted years ago.

Claude built a simple funky 3-chord foundation almost immediately. Then I recorded my own melody in real time and asked it to correct a few notes where I missed the timing or pitch. It handled that pretty well too.

What I like most is the division of labor. I still want to understand the parts of Ableton I actually use, but the assistant already knows much more about the mechanics of the DAW and can guide me through things I haven’t learned yet.

That matters because there is also a more existential problem here: we have limited time, but an almost unlimited number of skills we could learn. If you tried to master every tool, every interface, every theory, every technical detail before allowing yourself to create, you could spend something close to the lifetime of the universe just preparing.

So there is always a choice about where to spend attention.

For me, I’d rather use the assistant for more of the technical machinery and spend my limited time on melodic lines, harmonies, arrangements, improvisation, and the actual musical ideas I care about.

Back in the early 2000s, when I was thinking about making films, I imagined writing my own music for them too. That never really happened because I never developed a deep understanding of music theory or composition.

Now it suddenly feels much more achievable.

I’m not trying to become a professional composer or sell music. I’m doing it for myself: taking old melodies of mine, blending them with new ideas, maybe starting from a classical motif, transforming it, improvising over it, and using Claude as a musical copilot.

For me, that’s the exciting part: AI doesn’t remove choice. It changes the space of possible choices — and lets me spend more of my finite life on the parts of creativity I actually value.

text: quiet Claude Code / Agent SDK footgun (#80045): MCP server env secrets (GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN, Jira tokens, wiki bearers) get stuffed into --mcp-config JSON on the CLI argv. that means ps, /proc/*/cmdline, and EDR process logs can see plaintext tokens. confirmed pattern in @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk around 0.3.220. workaround shape: put mcp config in a 0600 file and pass the path, keep secrets out of argv, prefer child-only env. if your agent launcher prints its argv into a debug log, you already leaked the sprint's tokens.

Introducing Bursar: spending limits for AI agents, on @arbitrum.

Give your agent a budget, not your wallet.

The problem: agents now pay for data, other agents and even humans. Hand them a private key and one bad prompt can drain the wallet. Approve everything by hand and they aren't autonomous.

Bursar sits in the middle. You fund a vault, set the rules, and the smart contract enforces them:

- Per-payment and daily caps
- Owner approval above a threshold
- Recipient allowlist
- Task budgets with expiry
- Escrow for sub-agents and humans
- Every payment logged on-chain with a reason

Over a cap? Blocked, no funds move, and a PaymentBlocked event is logged, so you see what your agent tried to do.

We ran a real AI agent through it via an MCP server: it bought a data feed, locked escrow to hire a sub-agent, got blocked on a 150 purchase (and didn't retry), and a 60 payment waited for my approval.

203 tests, verified contracts, live dashboard, owner console and a playground to create your own vault.

text:
What if your AI agent didn't just learn from you…

but actually changed how it thinks, remembers, acts, and protects itself?

That's the idea behind OmniAgent.

It's an open-source agent framework built around something it calls OmniEvolve — full-dimensional self-evolution.

And this goes way beyond “the AI remembers your name.”

The agent can evolve:

→ Memory — turns explicit feedback and implicit signals into proactive memory
→ Skills — creates, inspects and repairs its own skills during use
→ Context — continuously adapts to your preferences and behavior
→ Brain Model — uses an online RL loop to improve the model itself

So the agent isn't just accumulating more data.

Its internal machinery is designed to keep changing.

But here's where it gets even crazier.

As the agent becomes more capable, its security layer is also designed to become harder to bypass.

OmniAgent uses a four-layer security pipeline:

LLM review → Policy engine → Human approval → Sandbox

And it has separate Sentinel and Guardian agents for planning and safety.

Then there's Deep Reflexion.

When something fails, it doesn't simply retry the same action.

It can analyze the failure, extract the underlying lesson, inject that insight back into its context, and try again.

So the bigger loop becomes:

Act → Fail → Understand → Adapt → Retry → Improve

That's a fundamentally different way of thinking about AI agents.

Most agents are built to execute tasks.

OmniAgent is experimenting with agents that evolve their memory, skills, context and reasoning while they're being used — while dynamically hardening their execution layer.

And it's open source.

The interesting question isn't:

“How capable is this agent today?”

It's:

“What does this agent look like after 10,000 interactions?”

text:
A sandbox founder just declared that Browserbase is dead, pointing to session pricing at a fraction of the cost. Whether that specific number survives contact with reality or not, the direction is real. Browser infrastructure for agents turned into its own crowded category almost overnight, Browserbase raised at a nine figure valuation, Cloudflare shipped Browser Rendering on its own edge network, and a wave of cheaper VM and container based alternatives showed up arguing the whole category is overpriced for what it does.

What gets lost in the pricing fight is that renting a headless Chrome instance was never the hard part of web automation. The hard part is what happens after the page loads. Sites change their markup constantly, and most scraping setups either break on every redesign or burn an LLM call re-reading the full page on every single run, which is slow and adds up fast at any real volume.

I built DeepScrape around a different split. An LLM looks at a page once, works out the extraction logic, and generates CSS selectors that get reused deterministically after that, so a redesign triggers a quick re-heal instead of a full re-think every time. It runs on Playwright, has a /map endpoint for discovering URLs across a site before you touch them, supports autonomous agent navigation for multi-step flows, and exposes the whole thing as an MCP server so Claude or Cursor can call it directly as a tool instead of you gluing together a scraper on the side.

Cheap browser compute solves infrastructure cost. It doesn't solve the part where your extraction breaks every time a site ships a frontend update.

text:
MCP gateways are quietly turning into the most important piece of enterprise agent infrastructure nobody outside platform teams has noticed yet, and Uber's internal setup is a good look at why.

The pattern is a control plane paired with a proxy gateway: a registry that knows about every internal service, and a gateway that translates MCP calls into whatever the service actually speaks, gRPC, Thrift, plain HTTP. New services get auto-discovered from existing API definitions instead of someone hand-writing a wrapper for each one. Every tool is disabled by default until a team explicitly turns it on, and every call gets checked against who's allowed to use it and scrubbed for anything that shouldn't leave the service boundary.

That's a very different shape from how most companies are still doing this, which is a developer standing up a one-off MCP server for whatever internal API they're touching that week. Block, Cloudflare, and Microsoft have all published versions of the same idea over the past year: don't expose services to agents one at a time, put a gateway in front of all of them and let the gateway handle auth, logging, and rate limits once.

The tradeoff nobody wants to say out loud is that the gateway becomes the thing you have to get right. A bug in one hand-built MCP server breaks one integration. A bug in the gateway, or a permission that defaults the wrong way, touches every agent talking to every service behind it at once.

Getting an agent to call an internal API was the easy part this year. Deciding, at scale, which agents get to call which APIs under what identity is turning out to be the actual work.

Every database GUI built before 2024 has the same problem now. It was designed for a human typing SQL by hand, and increasingly the thing querying through it is an agent that was never supposed to see a password prompt in the first place.

The part worth paying attention to is the Pro tier's MCP server: thirteen tools split across three permission levels, SQL sanitization before anything executes, row count estimates before a query runs, and a full audit log of every call an agent makes against your data.

It's not alone in trying to solve this. Google open sourced its own MCP Toolbox for Databases this year, a connector layer for the same problem at the infrastructure level rather than the GUI level. Beekeeper Studio and DBeaver are retrofitting AI panels onto interfaces that predate the agent era by half a decade. TablePlus still doesn't have a public MCP story. The gap between an AI assistant bolted onto an existing tool and a product built assuming an agent is a first class user from day one is where Gridex and Google's toolbox both sit, and it's a different design decision than most of the incumbents made.

What actually matters here isn't the query editor or the ER diagrams, every competitor already has those. It's the permission model. The moment you give an agent a live database connection, your security boundary stops being the login screen and starts being whatever the MCP server decides to allow, tier by tier, call by call. Most teams haven't thought about that yet. The tools shipping now are the ones that have.

text:
I wired Jev into my OpenClaw AI agent — then benchmarked it before and after. Here's the entire setup:

The problem: LLM agents are brilliant reasoners but terrible switchboards. Every judgment our agent's code had to consume — "is this test failure a harness bug, an app regression, or a flake?", "does this event deserve a reply or silence?", "is this action safe unapproved?" — forced a prose engine to emit structured decisions, then parse and pray. Slow, uncalibrated, occasionally silently wrong.

The fix: Jev — TypeSafe AI's System One model — wired into OpenClaw as the agent's fast-intuition layer. Typed questions (Choice / Score / Noul) → typed answers with calibrated probabilities. No prose. No parsing. Sub-second, ~450 tokens a call, content-addressed cache so repeat judgments are free.

How it plugs into OpenClaw (diagram below):
→ Gateway: jev-mcp registered as an MCP server, so Jev's judgment tools are first-class for the agent and every subagent it spawns. Key on disk — never in config, transcripts, or model context.
→ Policy: the agent's instruction file codifies deterministic-first: when code can determine the only legal action, no model call happens at all. Jev classifies only the genuine semantic choices among legal candidates.
→ Decision points: salience routing (reply / react / silent), external-send safety gates, expected-value action gating (probabilities from Jev, values from the owner's goals, arithmetic from code), and a calibration loop that logs agent-vs-Jev disagreements.
→ QA pipeline: every red e2e run auto-triages — failures grouped by error signature, classified harness / app-bug / env / flake / data, each with a player-impact score.
→ Memory: nightly dream cycles use Jev to decide which daily notes earn long-term memory, and whether each new friction event matches a growing error taxonomy or is genuinely novel.
→ Delegation: subagent deliverables are scored against their brief before anything gets relayed.

Confidence gates everything: ≥0.9 act + log · 0.6–0.9 act + flag · <0.6 escalate to the big model or the human.

The honest part — we benchmarked on real labeled incidents, including the agent's own mistakes:
• Attention routing: 50% → 92% ("before" was literally reply-to-everything — the exact spam humans notice)
• Memory triage: 75% → 100%; durable-fact detection 92% → 100%
• The calibration loop caught 1 of 1 genuine agent errors on its first run
• The self-eval harness scored a real past failure 0.69/3 with 92% redo-probability — it flags its own screwups before a human has to

Negative result included, because credibility matters: Jev scored 50% on workspace facts it cannot observe. It's a judgment classifier, not an oracle — so we feed it evidence, or restrict it to interpretation. Knowing what your tools can't do is part of the architecture.

Why this is an good move: intelligence isn't only reasoning horsepower. It's attention allocation, metacognition, memory consolidation, calibrated self-doubt. Humans already run this stack — fast intuition, slow deliberation, sleep-time consolidation. We're building the same one inside an agent (OpenClaw + Jev + qwen3.8-max), and graphing the progress weekly instead of vibes-checking it.

Fun detail: the agent built the benchmark datasets from its own incident log. Its favorite datapoint — routing a stale duplicate system event to "silent" at 96% confidence, the exact event class it used to spam the channel about.
