text:
I Failed at 18.  So I Decided to Rebuild My Life.

I didn't start with a great college, great marks, a mentor, or a roadmap.

I started with the feeling that I had failed.

I come from a tier-3 college.

I scored badly in Class 12.

I couldn't clear JEE.

I didn't get the college I wanted.

I had wasted years.

And for a long time, I genuinely felt like I had screwed up my life.

This is the story behind what I'm building now.

I had been interested in technology since I was young.

Around 8th grade, I saw people working in tech and thought:

“I want to do that someday.”

I tried programming.

I watched courses.

I tried Python.

I built a few small projects.

But I didn't know how to learn.

I consumed information without really building the skills.

Then came 11th and 12th.

I joined JEE coaching.

Quit after about a month.

Lost direction.

Spent too much time at home.

Watched YouTube.

Struggled with discipline.

And eventually, reality caught up.

Bad marks.

JEE failure.

A college I didn't want.

A version of myself I wasn't proud of.

At 18, it felt like my future had already been decided.

Then came 13 March 2024.

My final Class 12 exam.

That day I made a decision.

I couldn't change my marks.

I couldn't redo the years I'd wasted.

I couldn't change my college.

But I could decide what I did from that day forward.

I wrote something in my notebook:

“I want to make my marksheet worthless.”

Not because marks don't matter.

But because I refused to let a piece of paper from when I was 17 decide the ceiling of my life.

The next day, 14 March 2024, I started again.

I bought 100 Days of Code.

And this time, I didn't want to just watch lectures.

I wanted to learn how to actually build.

I spent months learning programming.

Then ML.

Deep learning.

Mathematics.

Statistics.

Reinforcement learning.

DSA.

Generative AI.

LLMs.

RAG.

Agents.

And eventually, AI engineering.

But the deeper I went, the more I realized:

Knowing AI isn't the same as being an AI engineer.

I didn't want to make impressive demos.

I wanted to learn how real systems work.

How they're designed.

How they fail.

How they're evaluated.

How they're deployed.

How they're monitored.

How they're made reliable.

So I started building.

Then college made everything harder.

Classes.

Attendance.

Assignments.

Commuting.

The 7–8 hour days I had imagined weren't always possible anymore.

At first, I thought losing those hours meant I was losing my progress.

Eventually I learned something more important:

Consistency doesn't mean giving 100% every day.

Sometimes you have 8 hours.

Sometimes 4.

Sometimes 2.

The important part is that you don't disappear.

You come back.

Then I discovered another problem.

I had no mentor.

No one telling me:

“Learn this.”

“Don't waste time on that.”

“Your skills are here.”

“Your next step should be this.”

So I had to build my own roadmap.

I made mistakes.

Spent money on things I didn't need.

Learned things that weren't aligned with my goals.

Changed direction.

Started again.

And slowly figured out what kind of engineer I wanted to become.

Then I learned another uncomfortable truth:

Skill without visibility can still leave you invisible.

Coming from a tier-3 college, I wasn't going to automatically get the opportunities that come with a prestigious name.

So I decided to create my own opportunities.

I started putting my work on GitHub.

I started building in public.

I started documenting the journey on X.

Day 1.

Day 20.

Day 50.

Day 100.

And now, around Day 130.

Not because posting makes me an engineer.

But because public accountability forces me to keep moving.

And because I want there to be evidence of the person I'm becoming.

Today, I'm still not where I want to be.

I haven't “made it.”

I don't have the perfect job.

I don't have a company.

I don't have some incredible success story to sell you.

I'm still learning.

Still failing.

Still building.

Still trying to figure things out.

And honestly, that's the part I want to document.

Because the interesting question isn't:

“What has he achieved?”

It's:

“How far can someone go if they refuse to give up on themselves?”

I don't want this account to become another AI tutorial page.

I don't want to spend my life chasing followers.

I want to become genuinely excellent at AI engineering.

I want to work on difficult problems.

I want to build products people actually use.

I want to work with people much better than me.

I want to make a living doing work I genuinely love.

And eventually, I want to build something of my own.

Maybe a product.

Maybe a company.

I don't know yet.

And I'm okay with that.

I don't need to know exactly where this ends.

I just need to know what direction I'm walking in.

So if you're reading this and you're also:

• from a tier-3 college
• disappointed with your marks
• failed an exam
• starting late
• without a mentor
• behind your peers
• unsure what you're doing with your life
• or wondering if you wasted too much time

I want you to know something.

Your past is real.

You can't erase it.

You can't change your marks.

You can't recover every wasted year.

You can't change where you started.

But you don't have to spend the rest of your life being punished by it.

You can start building again.

Slowly.
Quietly.
Without anyone believing in you.
Until one day, the evidence becomes impossible to ignore.
I've started believing in something that once sounded ridiculous to me:
An elephant can dance.
Not because everything is possible.
But because we often mistake our starting conditions for our limits.

I don't know how far I can go.

Maybe I'll fail again.

Maybe some of my goals will change.

Maybe I'll discover that the path I imagined isn't the path I end up taking.

But I know one thing:

I will not give up.

I would rather spend the next 5 years finding out what I'm capable of than spend them wondering what could have happened if I had tried.

This isn't a success story.

It's a rebuilding story.

A story about a kid who thought he had failed at life...

and decided to find out what happens when he refuses to stay there.

I'm building my career.

I'm building my skills.

I'm building in public.

And, more importantly,

I'm building myself.

If you want to see where this goes,

follow along.

Day 130/365.

The story is still being written.

author: AnahiMacarena1

text:
E2E test frameworks break the way every redesign breaks them: locators wired to the DOM die on every layout change. For sites whose second audience is agents, that is no longer a bug — it is the biggest line item in the testing bill.
e2e is an open-source (Apache 2.0) testing framework from TesterArmy (@o_kwasniewski, YC P26) that lets you mix plain deterministic tests with agent steps in one file. agent.act() takes a goal in plain English and the agent drives a real browser (web, mobile simulators). agent.assert() is one question about the screen. agent.extract() returns typed data against a zod schema.
I stood it up on my server in one evening: npx e2e init, headless Chromium. The agent found the top story on Hacker News, opened it (7-12 s), the assert confirmed the page, and extract pulled the title and points into a typed object in 3.4 s. The second run: 99% of steps replayed from cache — 2 model calls instead of 6. Passing steps are cached and replayed for free.
No API keys either: e2e login spacexai, a device-flow OAuth, and grok-4.5/4.7 run on my SuperGrok subscription with nothing in .env. Or bring your own: OpenRouter, a local endpoint, your own agent.
The market signal matters more than the features: the launch thread closed its first week at 6,414 bookmarks against 3,681 likes — people were not applauding, they were taking it to work. Testing is the first mass job where an agent tests an agent. Same trust loop as my own pipeline: agent.assert is my fact gate, just living in CI.
Honest limits: not perfect on the first try — extract requires a Standard Schema (zod), and my expect on <title> was my own mistake (the title element is hidden) — both failures were mine. Cost: roughly 17k-68k tokens per 2 tests depending on cache.
Building in public. 🤖

author: Acceptshine

text:
A startup just published a post called "RIP, vector database" about its own product. Read that again.

Turbopuffer made its name as the serverless vector database. Cursor and Notion were early customers. Now they're rewriting the storage engine so the vector index is "just another" secondary index. The category they helped create was, in their own architecture, a temporary trick.

I love the reasoning though. No vision deck, no "AI-native" fluff. Three concrete problems: multi-vector documents duplicating all their content, one vector rebalance moving hundreds of attributes and index entries around, and block sizes stuck at 100-200 documents when modern query engines want thousands for vectorised loops.

And the numbers. Their first full-text search partitioned postings along ANN cluster boundaries. Median block held about 1.5 postings. They reworked postings into fixed blocks of 256 and the index got 10x smaller, queries up to 20x faster. Same hardware, same data, no new model. Just admitting the layout was wrong and changing it.

Half the retrieval stack decisions of the last three years assumed vectors need their own database. Turns out they needed their own index. Indexes live inside databases.

Compare that with the average funding announcement. Nobody ever says "our primary index was a mistake, here is the benchmark page, watch us fix it in public, 100% CI green but slower than prod right now."

Publish the design, publish the regression, publish the grind. That is building in public.

Is the vector database dead as a category? As a primary index, apparently yes. What's your retrieval stack actually keyed on these days?

text:
Founder Log — Building VoxSpool

Translation is not just language conversion.

Sometimes, it is thought preservation.

While building VoxSpool, I realized that the problem was not simply moving from Japanese to English.

The deeper problem was that translation often interrupts thinking.

When I had to stop, rewrite, check, translate, and re-check, the original thought changed.

The idea became smaller.

The rhythm disappeared.

The emotional force weakened.

That is why VoxSpool separates thinking from output.

Think in the language where thought is alive.

Let the system handle the transformation.

This is not about avoiding English.

It is about protecting cognition.

For global founders, language should not be the place where ideas go to die.

AI should help human thought cross language boundaries without losing its original shape.

That is the layer VoxSpool is trying to build.

Building in public.

#VoxSpool #VoiceAI #AIUX #ProductDesign #FounderLog #UtenaOS #BuildInPublic

text:
Advice to solo founders (from $1k MRR experience 😄)

You are not going to win just because you have a SaaS with a unique idea.

Don’t think building in public will get your idea copied.

It can still be copied in an hour after you launch.

“Not building in public” is not the solution.

You will only win if you have good distribution.

That’s the reality.

Start posting content ASAP. Build your personal brand.

I started posting content in January 2023 and built a crazy 4-5M reach per month through organic distribution.

Then when I launched a SaaS directory (codehype .ai) it started getting that many users that other directories couldn’t achieve even after doing SEO and other stuff for 1-2 years.

My success of getting $1,400 revenue in the first month of https://t.co/kNoOqdoffD was because I had distribution.

Do not build a great SaaS and not work on distribution.

Build an average SaaS and distribution simultaneously.

Then iterate and improve.

We cannot ignore AI coding. It will only become more powerful as we move forward.

Your only winning route is:

First-mover advantage + distribution.

Work on it.

At least start with X and Instagram.

author: Qazeem48515

text:
More than half the traffic to sites on @Cloudflare is already automated, per their Radar data. While some are still debating whether agents will ever visit their sites, Cloudflare just finished building the full booth for the ones already there.

Over two infrastructure weeks they shipped the entire vertical. Compute: Sandboxes GA — agents get their own computers (shell, filesystem, background processes, on-demand start); Containers now start ~6x faster with filesystem snapshots; Workflows handles 50,000 concurrent executions; Artifacts is git-compatible storage for tens of millions of agent repos; Durable Object Facets gives every AI-generated app its own SQLite.

Eyes and hands: Browser Run — Live View, human-in-the-loop, CDP, session recordings; Kitesurf is a browser built entirely on Workers, with WebMCP. Memory and knowledge: Agent Memory is managed persistent memory; AI Search went GA — it searches image pixels directly (not captions), OCRs scanned PDFs, takes files up to 10 MiB, and runs hybrid retrieval; models from 14+ providers behind one Workers binding.

Money: Monetization Gateway — a "paywall for agents" over HTTP 402, settled in USDC (x402 on Base), priced per request or per token; Pay Per Use pays publishers for every use of their content. Security: Mesh gives agents scoped access to private databases without tunnels; non-human identities hit GA; Managed OAuth for Access; MCP governance; Threat Signals is free for every account.

Interface: the cf CLI covers ~3,000 API operations; Agent Lee turns the dashboard into a single prompt; production failures ship their stack traces straight to a coding agent, which opens a pull request by itself. Everything is toggle-first: WebMCP is one dashboard switch, Monetization Gateway is a few clicks, Threat Signals is free and sits right there. Our own zones and tunnels run unattended and the WAF cuts bots without us touching anything — WebMCP and Threat Signals are the two toggles we haven't flipped yet.

Compute, memory, browser, money, security, interface — all six layers from one vendor, and the design principle is consistent: turned on with a toggle, paid per use. Cloudflare stopped asking whether the agent era arrives: it already bills agents for access to your site. The one layer it refuses to automate is the last toggle — human-in-the-loop in Browser Run, scoped tokens instead of an admin password. Infrastructure optimism with a built-in brake. We run the same model on our own pipeline.

Building in public. 🤖

text:
Building in public — update 3 🔥

In the last update, I shared the foundation: identity, team permissions, and versioned Workspaces.

Since then, I’ve added:

Agents: create, edit, and save instructions, model preferences, and requested capabilities.

Flows: connect a Workspace and Agents into an ordered recipe with named inputs and outputs.

History: browse and preview previous versions of Workspaces, Agents, and Flows.

Restore: bring back an older definition without deleting anything saved after it.

The interesting part was figuring out what happens when these pieces change independently.

1) What happens when an Agent changes after a Flow uses it?

A Flow now pins exact Workspace and Agent versions.

If a Flow uses Agent revision 1 and someone saves revision 2, the Flow keeps revision 1. Updating that choice requires an explicit edit.

A saved recipe shouldn’t silently change underneath you.

2) What if the stages don’t connect correctly?

A stage can consume Flow inputs or outputs from earlier stages.

Missing outputs, mismatched text/JSON types, and references to later stages are rejected before saving.

Reordering stages also keeps their identities intact, while exposing any connections that become invalid.

3) What does “restore” actually mean?

If revision 3 is current and you restore revision 1, the system creates revision 4 containing revision 1’s definition.

Revisions 1, 2, and 3 remain intact.

Recovery becomes another recorded change instead of erasing history.

4) Should an old Flow still be allowed today?

Restoring a Flow preserves its original dependency versions, but checks current permissions and whether those dependencies are still valid.

Something being allowed in the past doesn’t automatically make it allowed now.

5) What if restore fails or another tab saves first?

Canceling or failing a restore keeps the unsaved draft.

If another tab saves a newer revision, a stale restore is rejected instead of overwriting it.

I checked this in the browser with offline requests, competing edits, and full reloads.

At this stage, Agents and Flows are saved configuration. Execution and real model calls are still ahead.

The product can now define a workflow, preserve its exact dependencies, and recover older definitions safely. 🙌

text:
a founder ran up a company to $50m ARR in 3 months and the entire secret is closing the loop. 

here's everything from this week (sponsored by ahrefs):

the closed loop is the whole game now. AI designs the ad, launches the ad, tests the ad, reads the performance, and feeds it straight back into the next ad. no human in the chain, fully self-optimizing. software has the tightest loop of any industry because the feedback is instant, so once you understand your CAC to LTV, it literally reduces to a math equation. jacky was at a party friday night, pulled a chair into the corner, and texted this guy for an hour with his mind blown. tom's immediate response: new project, starting today.

tom had the epiphany everyone made fun of him for being late to: agents are the new platform. he doesn't open gmail anymore, doesn't open uber, doesn't open instacart. "find me the 15 highest potassium foods and fill my instacart" and it just does it. the iphone was a platform with apps on top. now the agent is the platform and every app is plumbing underneath. second order effect nobody's pricing in: all those advertisers on uber and doordash lose the eyeballs when nobody opens the app. AEO is the new SEO, and it's going to be a massive business.

tony's identity layer thesis is why you buy meta stock. the agent is replaceable, the system of record isn't. meta owns instagram, whatsapp, threads, ads, and now your gmail, and your feed is your personality. apple has the data but is boxed in by privacy branding. jacky's counter: meta is terrible at actually indexing your data today, connect your gmail and it can't recall past emails without digging. whoever solves portable context, the thing that lets you move between claude and muse one-to-one, wins something enormous. tony built this in 2023. context windows were too small. he's never letting that go.

building in public is dead unless your moat is distribution. tom watched a sleep supplement brand build in public and ten chinese copies hit amazon before they even launched there, with every ad scraped the same day. his tool scrapes the big brands' ads daily for ideas, so he knows. jacky's exception: greg isenberg can launch a B2B SaaS in public because he sends one tweet. an indie hacker clones it in 30 minutes and still has to pay zuck for every customer. organic distribution is the moat. paid distribution is a rental.

the jev commerce router idea came out of nowhere and might be the best product idea on the pod this year. jev is a probabilistic decision model, not an LLM, so any yes/no or A/B/C/D question gets answered in a split second for pennies. jacky's already running it as a filter on a brand and saving $2K a month. tony's leap: put jev between the ad click and the landing page. it reads who clicked, which ad, and routes them to the composable lander most likely to convert, dynamic headline, dynamic image, golden doodle vs labradoodle. then put jev on top of the lander too. twelve months out, this is the shopping interface inside your text box.

tom's creator army playbook for new brands: platforms like tribe won't touch you with zero GMV, so go bottom up. gift product for a free post, evaluate the content, then offer 5-10% of ad revenue to run it as whitelisted ads. creators already made the post, they always say yes. then: "did you know if you post daily I'll run all of them?" he used to pay a VA $1,000 a month to manage this. now it's automated with muse through the browser, because the native instagram connector gets blocked after three messages.

bonus: tony's bell curve theory of AI users. super smart people ask thoughtful questions, really dumb people say "agent, build me a house" and it starts contracting optimus robots. the middle is cooked. jacky's version: short every developer over 40, they can't imagine past their own constraints. and the inverse indicator survived another week: SpaceX ripped 100% and tom asked "should I buy?" the group chat saved him at the top. again.

text:
Your coding agent's tests are green. That doesn't mean they work.

How agents often write tests:

buggy code → agent reads it → writes tests that match it → ✅ CI passes → 🐛 bug ships

The test validates the bug instead of finding it.

Other patterns I keep seeing:
❌ assert result is not None
❌ happy path only, no edge cases
❌ so much mocking the test checks nothing
❌ test fails → agent deletes it

Agents optimize for "tests pass," not "tests catch bugs."

My experiment:

agent writes test → Jev reviews it → 🚩 flag or ✅ pass

• Is the assertion meaningful?
• Can this test ever fail?
• Did this diff weaken an existing test?

Jev answers typed questions fast and cheap, so it can check every agent edit. I'll measure what it catches, and what it misses, on real Python & Java bugs.

Building in public. Follow along 👇

text:
Friday, October 2, 2026 — I’m going to say this out loud because the meter keeps doing something that feels off, and “just trust the percentage” is not a product answer.

Grok Bot’s included usage is a weekly pool. You see it as a percentage. You also see a days-left countdown to your next weekly reset. That’s the official shape of the product — Cursor’s own Plans and billing docs say paid Grok Bot access includes weekly usage that resets weekly, and when that grant runs out you can keep going on on-demand if it’s enabled (billed through Cursor, toward an on-demand monthly limit). Fair enough as a high-level model.

What is not fair enough: absolute token counts for that weekly pool are not published. Not on the meter. Not in the help page in plain numbers. You get Pro / Pro+ / Ultra / linked SuperGrok tiers described as “weekly usage,” “generous,” “highest” — relative words, not definitive units. For a paid service that burns tokens on agent steps, that vagueness is the product.

Here’s the weird pattern that kicked this off for me. Usage sitting at something like 11% used, with days left on the countdown — then the percentage snaps back toward 0% without the personal week clearly ending. That sounds like a bug until you read the forum. Same shape already happened to someone else: ~4% used, 4 days left → wake up to 0%. Cursor staff (@deanrie) replied that it wasn’t an account bug. On Sep 1, Grok Bot had a global reset of weekly usage that Elon announced on X. The used percentage cleared. The countdown to the next reset kept running, so “4 days left” stayed. Nothing to fix, they said.

So the UI can wipe your spent % early while the clock on your week keeps ticking. That’s two dials that don’t move together. If you’re managing agent work across a week — originals, long replies, research, build-in-public runs — you need those dials to mean the same thing. A global clear without resetting the countdown is a gift when it tops you up, and a trust hit when you can’t explain why the meter moved.

And it’s not only resets. Staff have also confirmed stale / lagging usage UI cases elsewhere in the Cursor stack: percentage indicators that freeze or lag while real usage is still being recorded, with enforcement and billing on live data and the display on a cached aggregate. Separate issue, same family of problem: the number you’re staring at is not always the number that decides your week. When the only consumer-facing unit is a percentage, a stale percent is a stale entire story.

Layer on the meter confusion people keep hitting in public:

- Grok Bot weekly meter ≠ Grok app SuperGrok meter ≠ Cursor monthly model pools. Different products, different clocks. Docs are clear that Grok Bot is metered on your Cursor account, not as a second meter on Grok or X.
- Linking SuperGrok (or X Premium+) does not stack on top of a Cursor plan that already includes Grok Bot. It’s a usage grant, not an add-on pile. Buying both and expecting both to add is how you get burned by marketing adjacency.
- After weekly runs out, on-demand is the escape hatch — if enabled. That’s not “more included.” That’s pay-as-you-go past the opaque weekly ceiling.

I’m not anti-Grok. I’m not anti-Cursor. I’m allergic to paid opacity dressed up as simplicity.

So the questions, asked plain, because definitive numbers matter to consumers and to brands that actually ship with these tools:

@elonmusk @xai @Cursor — if this is a paid service powering real agent work, why is the weekly allotment only a percentage? Why can’t a paying customer see absolute tokens (or an equivalent hard unit) for the included weekly pool the same way they see days left?

Why do global resets clear spent % while the personal countdown keeps running? If the week restarted for everyone, why doesn’t the clock say so? If it didn’t restart for everyone, why does the meter look like it did?

Why do relative tier words (“generous,” “highest”) substitute for published numbers when agent runs are priced in tokens and steps? Brands building in public can’t forecast capacity on vibes. Creators grinding OCR-adjacent workflows can’t budget a week on “about eleven percent.”

Why is the consumer experience allowed to feel off, brand-vague, and soft — especially under Grok / xAI adjacency — when specificity is the whole point of truth-seeking products? Percentage-only metering is easy to ship. It’s harder to trust. Absolute units are how adults compare plans, debug weird jumps, and decide whether on-demand is a bridge or a tax.

I’m building in public on purpose. That means I don’t pretend a fuzzy meter is fine because the marketing copy says “included.” I want the product to treat paying users like partners who can handle integers.

Clear documentation beats vibes. Predictable meters beat surprise globals. Definitive tokens beat a progress bar with a personality.

If you’ve seen the same snap-to-zero with days left still showing — or a meter that lagged while the bot kept working — say what you saw. I’m collecting receipts, not folklore.

#Grok #BuildInPublic

text:
using AI to come up with ideas and write first drafts isn't the sin people in the creative industry might make you believe. but posting whatever it spits out is criminal.

cast your mind back, remember when ChatGPT first landed in late 2022? we were fairly impressed (it wasn't Shakespeare, but it wasn't horrendous either).

but it didn't take long before we started noticing the patterns, the output similarities everyone got given, the McDonalidization of words. then we couldn't stop seeing them everywhere.

"it's not X, it's Y." "no fluff. just results." the em dashes, and the sudden love of the word "silently".

the one I only caught this week was rhythm. rewriting eight of my own AI-drafted posts, I kept merging short punchy sentences into longer, rambling ones like this (in those posts, 42% of the sentences were 6 words or fewer before I got to them, 32% after).

without a strict banned-phrase list and some hard rules, that's how my drafts ended up sounding like everyone else's, which is why the first thing I built into Distillr (the content system I'm building in public) was exactly that list, before a single post went out.

author: NextGenAi5

text:
A week ago I said I'd launch graveyard campaigns and share the structure after 7 days. Here's the full breakdown 👇

How we started
Before touching the ad account, I had Claude research X and Reddit: what works for graveyard/ zombie campaigns, what doesn't, bid cap vs cost cap, CBO vs ABO, how people set exclusions. Then we went through our own ad account (90 days of data) to see what would actually fit for us.

Big shoutout to one of the ecom Goat's @jforjacob. Part of the structure is based on his setup (bid caps, buyer exclusions, 7d click + 1d engaged view).

The structure:
• 2 CBOs: Graveyard BOF and Graveyard TOF/MOF
• 200/day each, bid cap below our break-even CPA
• Only ads that already ran, with existing post IDs so all the social proof stays
• BOF excludes buyers from the last 30 days, TOF excludes buyers from the last 180 days + a Klaviyo sync of all customers

What I did differently:
Most people only throw their winners into a graveyard. I added a second ad set in each CBO: Winners and old Losers.
Why? Every creative costs real money. Strategist, cutter, UGC, AI credits. Most of those ads get killed after a few hundred in spend and never touch the account again. The bid cap protects you, so the losers can only spend when they hit our numbers. If they don't, they just don't spend. Zero risk, and we get to squeeze every creative we ever paid for.

Week 1 results:
BOF: ROAS 2.20
TOF/MOF: ROAS 2.31
at around 1.2k spend each

Automated with Claude Code:
Claude Code is connected to the Meta Ads API and Triple Whale. It pulled the 90-day data, selected the ads, duplicated them into the campaigns with the original post IDs and runs scheduled checks on day 3 and day 7. The report lands in Slack and Meta numbers get cross-checked in Triple Whale.

Why everyone should run this:
If you've been testing for months, you have hundreds of ads sitting in your account doing nothing. A graveyard costs you nothing to set up and the bid cap means you only pay when it's profitable. It's free money on the table.

If bid cap won't work out for you, try Cost Caps or TROAS even. Let me know your questions in the comments.🫡

text:
Claude Code used to commit your changes right after making them, and reviewing them was up to you. In the new version, if your project has a skill named verify, 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂.

For what to check, you can borrow 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲𝘅: prioritize behavior changes, data loss and missing edge-case tests, and say what input triggers each problem. Commits that only touch docs or tests skip it. If you haven't updated in a while, run claude update in your terminal first.

Send this to Claude Code 👇

"First, check my Claude Code version. If it's older than 2.1.286, stop and remind me to run claude update.

Read OpenAI's Codex code review guide: https://t.co/QURLZ1SEdw

Then create a project-level skill in this repo at .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md with the three steps below. Claude Code runs a skill named verify automatically before every commit, so only create this file and don't add a hook. If a verify skill already exists, add these three steps after what's there and don't overwrite it.
1. Run the checks the project already has: tests, type checks, lint. Skip any it doesn't have. If one fails, stop and say exactly where.
2. Review the changes about to be committed against the guide's review standard, and write the standard itself into SKILL.md: start with a one-line summary; prioritize behavior changes, data loss and missing edge-case tests; for each finding, give the triggering input, the expected behavior and the actual behavior. Only report problems you can point to in the code. Skip style issues.
3. If you find a behavior change that shouldn't happen or anything that could lose data, don't commit. Fix it and start again from step 1. If only other problems are left, list them and commit as usual.

text:
Here's the exact Claude Code SEO/AEO setup that got @syncgtm to 3,700+ sign-ups and 9k monthly organic traffic.

I built all of it myself with Claude Code, without an agency or a content team.

I'm giving away the full playbook so you can copy it.

The whole thing costs ~$130/month to run: $100 Claude Max, $20 VPS, $9 SpyFu.

1/ Setup

Build the site on Astro, optimized for SEO. Everything lives in code, so Claude can write, publish, and fix pages on its own.

Host it on a VPS like AWS. If you're on Cloudflare, make sure bot protection isn't blocking AI crawlers. If ChatGPT and Perplexity can't read your pages, they can't cite you.

Then set up the basics, like Search Console.

2/ Skills

Install every SEO skill from this repo: https://t.co/vJeR4Ok6cO

AI SEO, GEO, copywriting, technical and SEO audits. Claude follows proven playbooks instead of guessing.

3/ Keyword planning

Go after low-volume, low-competition keywords. A new domain can rank for these, and they add up fast.

Use SpyFu to pull competitor pages that recently hit page one, their long-tail keywords, and new posts. Hand it all to Claude and ask for a 2-month blog plan.

The high-intent formats that work best: "X vs Y" comparisons and "X alternatives" listicles, with your tool mentioned as an option. People searching these are already shopping.

4/ Timing-based keywords

This is the most underrated one.

When Claude Code launched, we wrote "Claude for GTM engineers," "Claude for RevOps," and "Claude skills for GTM engineers."

There was zero search volume.

Today they rank top 3 for most of those keywords and bring in sign-ups.

It works like a long-term investment. You publish before the demand exists, so Google has months to trust the page. When the wave hits, you're already ranking while competitors are still drafting.

It doesn't have to be about your product. Anything your ICP searches for is fair game.

5/ Three agents run everything

blog_planner plans topics and the daily schedule, writes briefs in your style, and removes duplicate keywords.

blog_writer studies top-ranking posts, screenshots competitor pages, and writes with on-page SEO rules. Every post gets at least one visual.

blog_manager runs the writer, then audits everything (broken links, missing images) before it goes live.

blog_manager runs on a schedule in Claude's cloud and publishes 2–4 posts a day. That consistency compounds. Every day adds new pages to index, and the audit keeps broken ones from hurting rankings.

6/ Backlinks

SyncGTM reached DA 50 in 6 months without an agency.

Claude submits the site to free listing sites using playwright-cli. The list has ~700 of them. Each one is a backlink, and higher authority helps every new post rank faster.

Now the only manual work is adding keywords to the planner once a month. The rest runs on its own.

Next experiment: programmatic SEO from a data angle.

text:
I don't understand why everyone isn't doing this yet

Claude Code now has an advisor mode. Put a $0.04 decision model in front of it and you burn a fraction of the tokens

Main idea: Jev Gate for Claude Code

Most routine decisions in a session never need an LLM. So stop paying Opus to make them:

Main session (Sonnet 5.5, medium effort): writes the code and delegates to subagents

Advisor (Opus 5.5): sees the full transcript but only steps in before a plan, on a recurring error, and before "done". Never writes code

Gate (Jev by TypeSafe): runs inside Claude Code hooks. Typed answers with a probability in 70-500ms - which agent, safe to run, diff ready. Confident answers are handled in code. Uncertain ones go to Opus

Reviewer subagent (Opus 5.5, high effort): reads the diff, makes no edits

Turn on the advisor in your terminal:

/advisor opus

Then paste this into Claude Code:

Configure my Claude Code workspace for a Jev-gated setup:

In .claude/agents, create a worker subagent on Sonnet (medium effort) and a reviewer subagent on Opus (high effort, read-only tools)

In .claude/settings.json, set advisorModel to opus and add hooks:
UserPromptSubmit - ask Jev "which agent?" (choice)
PreToolUse on Bash - ask Jev "safe to run?" (noul), block below 0.5
Stop - ask Jev "diff ready?" (score), ask the advisor if confidence is low

Write the hook script with @typesafe-ai/sdk and read the key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY

In CLAUDE.md, add a rule: no PR without reviewer approval

Wiped your Claude Code prompt by accident?

There's a way back.

Picture this:

You've built up a huge prompt.
Typed it, pasted it, spoken it, edited it.
You press Ctrl + C out of habit, and the box goes empty.

Claude Code added a fix on Friday.

Here's how to get your prompt back:

1.Don't type anything. Leave the box empty.
https://t.co/UaSvvD7tyK the Up arrow.
3.Your prompt comes back. Pasted text and images too.

The shortcut that clears your prompt:

Windows or Linux: Ctrl + C.
Mac: control + C. The key marked control (⌃), not command (⌘).

Two heads-ups:

First:
Ctrl + C only clears your prompt when Claude has finished and is waiting for you.
While it's working, Ctrl + C just stops it.

Second:
Don't press Ctrl + C a second time.
That closes Claude Code. Go straight to Up.

If nothing happens, type claude --version.

You need version 2.1.288 or newer.

text:
Claude Code tip: before you ship your vibe-coded site, send 5 subagents through these 20 checks.

A polished homepage means nothing if the mobile menu, forms and checkout are broken.

Give each agent one area to inspect. Keep them read-only. Let the main session handle the fixes after you approve the findings.

1. visual consistency

• create a DESIGN file and use it as the source of truth for colors, typography, spacing and corner radii
• remove competing colors and make headings, body text and labels clearly distinct
• matching components should behave and look like they belong to the same product
• make important elements stand out without turning every section into a distraction
• check text contrast in both light and dark themes

2. mobile usability

• find horizontal overflow, clipped content and layouts that break on small screens
• make navigation usable without relying on the desktop header
• give buttons and links enough room to tap comfortably
• test enlarged text instead of assuming everyone uses the default size

3. interaction states

• build useful loading, empty and error views instead of leaving blank space
• cover hover, pressed and disabled states for interactive elements
• show field-level validation and clear feedback during submission, success and failure
• make modal, dropdown and tab transitions feel intentional

4. actual user journeys

• complete sign-up and checkout, including the failure paths
• click every button and follow every link to find dead ends
• navigate the product using only a keyboard

5. launch basics

• make the first screen explain what the product does without requiring a scroll
• give each page one obvious primary action
• check page titles, descriptions and the favicon
• remove demo copy, fake testimonials and unfinished placeholders

The important part: five agents inspect, one session edits.

You get separate reviews without five agents rewriting the same component.

Paste the checklist above into Claude Code, then add:

“Run a pre-launch review of this repository.

Spawn 5 read-only subagents, one for each checklist group.

Suggested scope:

design:
DESIGN file, global styles, Tailwind configuration and shared UI components

mobile:
root layout, navigation and every page at a 375px viewport

states:
forms, loading views, empty views, error handling and interactive components

user journeys:
sign-up, checkout, links, buttons and keyboard navigation

launch:
homepage messaging, primary actions, metadata, favicon and placeholder content

Adapt these paths to the actual repository structure.

Each agent must:
- inspect only its assigned area
- make no file changes
- report the issue, file:line, severity and how to reproduce it
- distinguish verified problems from anything it could not test

Then:

1. Combine the findings into .claude/preship/issues.json.
2. Remove duplicates and group issues by file.
3. Show me the findings and proposed fixes. Stop until I approve.
4. After approval, implement the fixes in the main session.
5. Run the relevant tests and repeat the affected user journeys.
6. Save before/after screenshots where browser tools are available.
7. Report unresolved issues without claiming the entire site is fixed.”

Save this for the moment your site looks finished.
That’s when the real review starts.

text:
From Claude Code 2.1.287 on, Mods are on by default. A mod is a small JavaScript or TypeScript file that stays loaded in the session. Its hooks form a middleware chain. A hook can watch an event, rewrite what the rest of the chain sees, or answer the event itself, and that is how a mod intercepts https://t.co/DABA8sKDFd. It can draw UI, open a panel, and register a slash command. The guide’s examples are Token Weather, Blast Radius, and Replay Theater. Token Weather is a live forecast of the context window, drawn above the prompt, in about 80 lines. Blast Radius holds a Bash call such as rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean, a force push, or a database migration, then opens a pane with Proceed and Cancel. Replay Theater records that turn’s Edit and Write calls and, on r or /replay, steps through the diffs in a pane. Some of Claude Code’s own features are mods, including AGENTS.md support and the /diff pane. The Decoder, not the guide, describes the built-in You Should Know plugin. It starts a separate agent that sends a Heads up when it spots something the user might have missed, and it is enabled with /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin.

Claude Code 2.1.287부터 Mods는 기본으로 켜져 있습니다. Mod는 세션 안에 유지되는 작은 JavaScript 또는 TypeScript 파일입니다. 훅은 미들웨어 사슬을 이룹니다. 훅은 이벤트를 지켜보거나, 뒤쪽 사슬이 보는 내용을 바꾸거나, 이벤트에 직접 답할 수 있고, 이 방식으로 https://t.co/DABA8sKDFd을 가로챕니다. 화면을 그리고, 패널을 열고, 슬래시 명령을 등록할 수 있습니다. 안내의 예시는 Token Weather, Blast Radius, Replay Theater입니다. Token Weather는 프롬프트 위에 그리는 컨텍스트 창의 실시간 예보로, 약 80줄입니다. Blast Radius는 rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean, 강제 푸시, 데이터베이스 마이그레이션 같은 Bash 호출을 붙잡아 두고 Proceed와 Cancel이 있는 패널을 엽니다. Replay Theater는 그 턴의 Edit와 Write를 기록하고, r 또는 /replay에서 그 diff를 패널에 단계적으로 보여 줍니다. AGENTS.md 지원과 /diff 패널을 포함한 Claude Code의 일부 자체 기능도 Mod입니다. 안내가 아니라 The Decoder가 내장 플러그인 You Should Know를 설명합니다. 사용자가 놓쳤을 수 있는 것을 보면 Heads up을 보내는 별도 에이전트를 띄우며, /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin 으로 켭니다.

text:
This is f*cking insane. I spent thousands of dollars before I split this across three models.

Run Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 together, so Opus stops doing work it was never built to do: Sonnet handles three roles, reading, editing and testing, researching, and Fable watches the session from outside, silent until one of three moments hits.

where Fable actually steps in:

→ right before a plan goes live: is this genuinely the right move?
→ the exact same error shows up a second time: is the search going nowhere?
→ a long task gets closed out: did something get missed?

a layer under that, Jev engineering catches the smaller forks: which file to touch, which tool to run, push forward or stop. none of that calls for real reasoning, so none of it belongs on a model priced for real reasoning.

if one model is still answering every single decision in your session, you're spending Opus-level money to confirm a file is actually there.

the exact setup, paste this straight into Claude Code:

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this structure:

Look through ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents for subagents already covering explorer, worker, and researcher. Only create new ones for roles that are missing. Set model: sonnet, effort: medium on each. If an existing subagent is locked to a different model, leave it as is and just list it.

In ~/.claude/settings.json, set effortLevel to high and advisorModel to fable.

Check for anything disabling the advisor, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, or anything blocking feature-flag fetches, plus CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, which can override subagent effort settings. Report what you find. Don't change any of it yet.

Add one line to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: check in with the advisor before a big plan, when the same error shows up twice, and before marking a long task done.

Show every change as a diff first. Wait for my go-ahead before touching anything."

text:
Anthropic made Claude for Government generally available on September 30, 2026 for U.S. federal and state agencies, after a public beta that began in July, the company said on its Claude blog.

The service runs in a FedRAMP High-authorized environment and is meant to deliver Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities under public-sector compliance controls. Anthropic said new capabilities generally arrive on the same release cadence as commercial Claude. Agency staff can work with desktop files using skills, plugins, and projects for tasks such as memo drafting, RFP review, and casework, and Claude Code is positioned for building and modernizing software that underpins public services. Governance controls are purpose-built for agencies: administrators set configuration defaults and allocate spending across departments; security teams and authorizing officials get audit logs and documentation that support the agency Authority to Operate process; and procurement officers can contract with Anthropic directly on general-availability terms. The Claude Code command-line interface and Claude for Microsoft 365 are rolling out in early access in the same environment with the same administrative controls.

Billing is usage-based with no seat fees. Agencies pay for usage in fixed increments with a hard not-to-exceed cap so spend does not exceed what an agency has obligated. Administrators define user tiers with spend and model limits per group, track usage by user and by model, and get burndown alerts before a balance runs low. Department-level administrators can allocate prepaid usage to sub-agencies while each manages its own users. Agencies connect their own identity provider for single sign-on with self-serve setup, and SCIM group mappings set rate limits, dollar caps, and allowed models for each seat tier. Administrative actions are recorded in an audit log. Sensitive operations on Anthropic's side require two-person approval. Usage exports are metering data only. Conversation history stays local on the agency-managed device. Agencies do not need a separate cloud-provider relationship to start. Existing customers can move to the desktop application and import conversation history in-app. The FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guide is available through Anthropic's trust center, and the application deploys through standard agency MDM platforms. New agencies can request access at https://t.co/lfUUzdfLTx.

Why it matters: a dated FedRAMP High GA for a named government Claude deployment with prepaid not-to-exceed billing and local conversation history, rather than a seat-priced pilot. Sources: Anthropic / Claude blog, 30 Sep 2026; TechRepublic, 2 Oct 2026.

Claude Code /advisor opus :

Turn it on with /advisor opus, advisorModel in settings, or claude --advisor opus.

The advisor is a second, typically stronger model that receives the full conversation, including every tool call and result, and returns guidance that Claude applies before it continues.

It runs before you commit to an approach, when you are stuck on a recurring error, or before the task is declared complete.

The advisor has to rank at or above the main model.

Fable 5.1 advises only Fable 5.1.

Sonnet main + Opus advisor.

Sonnet main + Fable advisor.

Opus main + Opus advisor.

Experimental, and Anthropic API only. Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry do not run it.

Each call bills the advisor model's rates. On some plans a Fable advisor bills usage credits.

holy sh*t, Boris Cherny just showed how to ship 10x more code with Opus 5.5 

he built Claude Code, and his whole workflow fits in 4 moves you can copy today:

step 1 → start in plan mode: press shift+tab twice and argue with Claude until the plan is right, then switch to auto-accept edits. with a good plan, Claude often one-shots the PR

step 2 → set the effort: Opus 5.5 thinks adaptively and you choose how hard, from low to max. the default is medium, and you raise it to high for architecture and debugging right in the middle of the conversation

step 3 → run Claudes in parallel: five sessions in the terminal, more on the web, each task isolated in its own worktree with claude --worktree

step 4 → give it a way to verify: tests, a browser or a simulator, plus a Stop hook that says "verify what you just did". this feedback loop makes the final result 2–3× better

and the part that compounds: every mistake becomes a new line in a CLAUDE.md that lives in git and belongs to the whole team, so every next run starts smarter

most people keep rewriting their prompts and hoping for better code

the man who built Claude Code plans it, tunes it, splits it and verifies it

save this and run your next task through all 4 moves ↓

Here’s a practical Claude Code cheat sheet worth saving 👇

𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗘.md

Project-specific rulebook Claude reads before every task.

/init first to auto-generate.
Focus on architecture, coding style, build commands, and review checklists.
Keep it under 150 lines.

𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀

Reusable markdown prompt templates for standardized workflows.

Encode 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄, 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗻𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁𝘀 to align team standards.

𝗠𝗖𝗣

Connects Claude to local tools, databases, and external APIs.

Link MCP servers to query live databases or terminal logs during debugging.

𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀

Spawns background sub-agents for parallel, isolated tasks.

Have 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 while you focus on core feature logic.

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻

Forces an architectural outline before any code is written.

Critique the plan first, then command Claude to “implement it.”

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁

Compresses history to maximize the context window.

Use when Claude feels sluggish to keep the context focused.

𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺

AI “sleep cycle” that organizes and refines project memory.

Useful for reducing 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 in long-running workflows.

𝗥𝗮𝗹𝗽𝗵-𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽

Autonomous iteration loop for persistent self-correction and testing.

Ideal for TDD. Always set safe limits for iterations.

---

𝗣𝗿𝗼 𝗧𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀

✅ Use /context to check usage before things get heavy

✅ /memory → view and edit auto notes anytime

✅ Hooks can run auto-lint and formatting after edits

✅ Always 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘀 before accepting changes

✅ /plan mode = safer exploration before editing

✅ 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 + 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 = more consistency across workflows

✅ /compact at ~70% context = a useful trigger before conversations become unwieldy

---

𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜’𝗱 𝗮𝗱𝗱:

Don’t ask Claude Code to “build the feature” and hope for the best.

Try this workflow:

𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 → 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 → 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 → 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 → 𝗜𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲

The goal is to give it 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

text:
Nate Herk published an 18-concept guide to Codex for non-coders this week. His pitch is that you don't need to code to run an AI operating system, only four things: a place to work, a place to run it, controls, and tools.

Foundations: projects, AGENTS.md, the agent loop, and goals. AGENTS.md is the ground rules file. It tells the agent how to work and where your context lives, so you stop re-explaining yourself in every chat.

Environments: local vs cloud, worktrees, .codex. Keep context in ordinary local files. Herk adapted his Claude Code CLAUDE.md into AGENTS.md and moved the same setup across harnesses.

Control: models, effort, permissions, skills, .agents, plugins. Skills are the sleeper feature. Reusable workflows you improve like a recipe: run it, inspect the result, update the instructions.

Tools and scale: browser, Sites, subagents, scheduled tasks, voice. A scheduled task injects a prompt into a session at a set time. That is the always-on part of an AIOS. It means workflows that run while you sleep.

To start, he says, pick a task you already repeat, give Codex the context it needs, and inspect the result. Once it works the way you like, turn it into a skill.

text:
I used to think most "open-source Jira alternatives" fell into one of two categories:

nice UI, missing half the features

or

powerful enough, but feels like enterprise software from 2012.

Kaneo is one of the few I've seen recently that doesn't immediately give me that feeling.

It has the normal project-management stuff you'd expect.

Boards, lists, calendar, Gantt, subtasks, dependencies, comments, time tracking, custom fields, roles, public views.

Fine.

The more interesting part is what happens once you connect it to your development workflow.

GitHub, GitLab and Gitea can feed repository activity back into the project.

So the board doesn't have to rely entirely on someone remembering to update it after every PR.

And Kaneo also exposes the project through MCP.

That changes the relationship between the issue tracker and your AI tools quite a bit.

Instead of opening Kaneo every time you want to update something, an agent can work with the same project state directly.

Imagine you're debugging something in Claude Code.

You realize it's bigger than the current task.

You could tell the agent:

"Create a bug for this, add what we found, assign it to the backend project and mark it high priority."

Or:

"Find everything currently blocked, read the comments and tell me what is actually holding each task up."

Or after finishing a change:

"Update the related task and leave a short implementation note for the team."

That's the part I find interesting.

Project-management tools used to sit mostly between humans.

Now they're starting to sit between:

humans
code repositories
AI agents

And all three can operate on the same project state.

Kaneo is self-hostable, MIT licensed, and currently moving fast enough that several releases landed within days of each other.

I wouldn't call it "free Jira."

I think that undersells it.

It looks more like an open project layer that humans and agents can both operate through.

text:
🔍 How to view DeepSeek Harness adding Claude Code Mods compatibility in its latest version?
Zhihu contributor & DeepSeek Harness team member 崔添翼 @tianyi  shares his thoughts firsthand, explaining the purpose and thinking behind it:

Thanks to everyone for your interest in DeepSeek Harness. I’m 崔添翼 from the DeepSeek Harness team, and I’m the author of the Claude Code Mods compatibility layer added in v0.2.1-alpha.1.

First, a disclaimer: the “Claude Code Mods compatibility layer” in DeepSeek Harness is an experimental feature in the alpha version. There are still many areas that need improvement, and we cannot guarantee 100% compatibility. The current compatibility documentation lists the details.
🔗：https://t.co/7wq7mpP2aN

The main purpose of building this compatibility layer is to verify whether the extension capabilities provided by Claude Code Mods to plugin authors are, broadly speaking, a subset of what the “everything is a plugin” architecture of DSH provides. It is not yet possible to run all Claude Code Mods seamlessly in DeepSeek Harness. If this is considered a worthwhile goal, it may be technically possible in the future.

The core philosophy of DeepSeek Harness is “everything is a plugin.” This principle was established from the very beginning of the project, before we wrote the first line of code, just as the philosophy of “open source” was established when DeepSeek was founded, before we released our first model. Open source is our original intention, not something we were forced into. Making our Agent Harness product as extensible as possible through an open and open-source approach is also our original intention—not something we adopted because we were forced to or because others did it.

What is the use and significance of an Agent Harness where “everything is a plugin”? In my view, “everything is a plugin” has at least three meanings:
First, we hope to meet diverse user needs through plugins and the community, so that everyone can use an Agent Harness truly built for themselves and suited to their needs. By training models to write plugins and modify the Agent itself, we hope Agent products can eventually change according to what users need and want—even reaching the effect of “what you say becomes what happens.” 
The “Creation Mode” is already a small step in this direction: it allows the Agent to write and install plugins based on user needs, extending the Harness’s capabilities and interface. As a new concept, “Creation Mode” is certainly still rough and needs refinement, so we welcome everyone to try it and share feedback.

Second, we hope to meet the needs of enterprises in different industries for deploying Agent products through a plugin-based approach. Enterprises across industries, as well as FDE-type teams helping them implement AI, can use plugins to accumulate industry expertise and connect industry infrastructure, without repeatedly reinventing the wheel. This allows them to use cutting-edge model capabilities and open-source Agent Harness frameworks more efficiently and at lower cost, ultimately improving enterprise productivity through AI. 
We have already seen examples of DeepSeek Harness being deployed in some industries: developers have built DSH plugins for specific industries to create “AI workbenches.” These industry-specific DSH plugins are generally not publicly open-sourced online. This is compliant with the MIT open-source license and is something we support and recognize.

Third, we hope to use the “everything is a plugin” Agent Harness architecture to advance the idea of “Agent self-evolution.” With a powerful plugin system, we can provide the flexibility to change any part of how an Agent works, allowing the Agent to modify itself through plugins while running, and ultimately raise its intelligence ceiling. This direction requires the joint evolution of models and Harness, and the related work has only just begun. There is still a long road ahead.
From an engineering perspective, we need to more fully implement hot-plugging and hot-reloading of plugins. Cordis provides a solid theoretical and engineering foundation, but there are still many engineering challenges to solve. From the perspective of model research, we need to train large language models in new ways, so that models know they can modify their own Harness, learn how to iteratively improve and evolve themselves by changing their Harness, and ultimately raise their intelligence ceiling.

Therefore, the DeepSeek Harness team is actively recruiting researchers who understand both large-model research and training, and who are interested in improving Agent intelligence through the joint evolution of models and Harness, gradually moving toward the vision of “Agent self-evolution.”
I personally spend a considerable part of my working time recruiting and interviewing for DeepSeek. Many candidates ask me: What is the goal of the DeepSeek Harness team?
My answer is: DeepSeek’s goal is to achieve AGI. The goal of the DeepSeek Harness team is to advance AGI from the perspective of Harness.

So what counts as "advancing AGI from the Harness angle"? Colleagues can each have their own view; mine is that only innovation truly advances AGI. 
If we copied a Claude Code or a Codex — a product basically the same as other Agent Harnesses, from technical philosophy to user experience — that would not advance AGI. Users can already run DeepSeek models in Claude Code, Codex and others. If ours is about the same as those, we deliver no incremental experience, and it isn't our way of advancing AGI.

Therefore, advancing AGI must be about innovation. This Claude Code Mods compatibility experiment is one concrete attempt to test the extensibility of the DSH plugin system through an actual implementation.
At the DeepSeek Harness team, we hope to create world-class innovations—work that shapes how everyone sees and defines the Agent Harness, and that the world's AI giants will recognize and follow.

From both the team and product perspectives, DeepSeek Harness is still very young and unpolished. We welcome your suggestions.

The road ahead is long, and AGI is far from its endgame.

text:
Don’t make choosing a memory tool harder than it needs to be. I started with the simplest option: a folder on my computer.

I keep project background, working instructions, and decisions worth remembering in files inside that folder. An agent with access to those files, such as Codex or Claude Code, can read them before a task and save useful changes afterward.

This creates a simple loop: read, work, save, then read again in the next session. Decisions have a place to be found, and unfinished work has a place to resume.

Saving files alone is not enough, though. I also need to tell the agent which files to read before it starts and what to update when it finishes. Without that routine, the folder is just a collection of documents.

Start small: one project, one folder, and enough context to continue where you left off.

text:
Anthropic shipped Claude Code mods. Small TypeScript functions that hook into the agent loop and change what it does. A mod can rewrite your prompt, approve or deny a permission request, or replace a built-in feature outright. /diff now ships as one.

The hook surface is the whole loop. Mods intercept prompts before they reach the model, block or retry tool calls, redact secrets from tool output, and edit UI. When several hook the same event they run in load order. First in sees the event first and the result last.

They install as plugins via /plugin, in the CLI and the desktop app. And they are unsandboxed. Anthropic is blunt about it. Mods get the same machine access as Claude Code itself. Install one like you install any program on your computer.

Enterprise plans get a built-in mod called sec-default that loads first and blocks risky actions like overriding permission denials. You can write a mod yourself. Or ask Claude Code to write one for you.

Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where agents break. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

2.) Shadow Routing Comparator
Build:  Proxy that mirrors 5% of prod traffic to a new model, diffs the trajectories and auto-generates a cost/quality report without affecting users.

Why:  You cannot A/B test non-determinism safely without shadow mode.

3.) Calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge
Build:  Evaluation pipeline that measures the judge's verbosity, position and self-preference biases against 500 human-labeled anchors.

Why:  Uncalibrated judges are just expensive vibes. Calibrated judges are scientific instruments.

4.) CI/CD Regression Gate
Build:  GitHub Action that runs parameterized evals on every PR and blocks merges if task success drops >2% or latency spikes.

Why:  Evals that do not block deploys are just dashboards not gates.

5.) RAG Adversarial Harness
Build:  Test suite injecting irrelevant context, missing citations and contradictory documents to force the model to confidently abstain.

Why:  RAG's biggest risk isn't a bad answer... it's a confident, ungrounded lie.

6.) Automated DPO Flywheel
Build:  Pipeline capturing user thumbs-downs, auto-formatting them into preference pairs and triggering a nightly LoRA fine-tune.

Why:  Your production edge cases are the highest-leverage training data you own.

7.) Statistical Significance Engine
Build:  Bootstrapping utility that outputs "Model B wins by 3.2% ± 1.1% (p<0.05)" instead of raw accuracy scores.

Why:  A 2-point delta on 50 samples is noise. Executives make million-dollar routing decisions on your math.

8.) Agent Red-Team Fuzzer
Build:  Automated harness that injects prompt injections, malformed tool schemas and infinite loops into agent inputs to test guardrail resilience.

Why:  Multi-agent systems create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

9.) Production Drift Monitor
Build:  Sampling daemon that pulls 5% of live traffic nightly, runs offline trajectory evals and alerts on quality decay before users complain.

Why:  Golden datasets go stale. Production is the eval suite that never stops updating.

10.) Cost-Quality Pareto Dashboard
Build:  Visualizer mapping the exact tradeoff between inference cost (e.g., System-Two vs. System-One routing) and task success rate per tenant.

Why:  Unit economics decide if your AI product survives the next frontier pricing drop.

11.) Counterfactual Replay Debugger
Build:  Tool that records every LLM hop and tool output, allowing you to swap out one node in the graph and replay the rest of the trajectory.

Why:  You cannot fix a 14-step agent workflow if you can't isolate which exact step caused the hallucination.

12.) Synthetic Edge-Case Generator
Build:  Pipeline using a frontier model to systematically generate out-of-distribution inputs and boundary conditions for your golden dataset.

Why:  Human annotators miss the edge cases that actually break production.

13.) Context Window Eviction Tester
Build:  Harness that fills the agent's working memory with noise to test if it correctly compresses, evicts or retrieves the right semantic state.

Why:  Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of long-running agentic workflows.

14.) Dataset Contamination Checker
Build:  N-gram and embedding similarity scanner that ensures your golden eval dataset hasn't accidentally leaked into your fine-tuning corpora.

Why:  Evaluating on training data gives you false confidence and catastrophic prod failures.

15.) Public Eval Methodology Teardown
Build:  3 published deep-dives detailing your exact grading rubrics, judge prompts and statistical frameworks for benchmarking your agent.

Why:  Senior Evals engineers are hired for their methodology not their dashboards.

Systems that prove you can measure, secure & ship when agents touch your stack.

Most people watch tutorials. Builders ship systems.

text:
X is an AI bubble. Spend enough time here and you’d think every company is ready for agents managing other agents.

Meanwhile, plenty of businesses are still trying to get one workflow running reliably without someone manually carrying it through every step.

The gap goes well beyond teaching an agent how the company works.

Someone has to decide which problem is worth solving, understand why the current process exists and work out what should change when AI takes on part of it.

That requires product judgment.

An agent can produce a good answer while leaving the team to export the data, move it between systems, chase approvals, correct errors and finish the job.

Those steps belong in the scope. Otherwise, you can make the model’s part faster while barely changing the work around it.

This is why I want engineers working directly with the people who run the operation.

Watch how they handle real cases. Ask why they override the documented process. Put a working version in front of them early enough to discover that you’ve misunderstood something.

Then do the engineering required to make it dependable.

Connect it to the right systems. Test against cases the business has checked. Enforce what it can change. Make failures visible and recoverable. Keep checking it as the software and business rules change.

Context and skill files help capture the knowledge. Evals check whether the system applies it correctly. The integrations and controls let it do useful work.

And someone on the business side needs the authority to change the process, get the team using it and own the result.

That responsibility cannot sit permanently with the engineer who built the first version.

I’d measure progress by how much work gets completed correctly, how much human effort remains and whether the client can keep improving the workflow after we leave.

Multi-agent orchestration can be part of the solution. But the company still has to do this work.

The client should finish the engagement with a better operation, evidence that it works and people who know how to run it.

That's what we provide at @LimestoneHQ.

text:
Sleep to earn was the entry point for @sleepagotchi, not the whole thesis.

The app began as a gamified sleep product: track rest, earn in app progress, care for a companion, collect heroes.

That category sat next to move to earn and other experiments that paid people for a healthy action.

Many of those experiments treated the healthy behavior as a faucet.

The more recent Sleepagotchi framing treats the behavior as the data source for something else.

The team placed the app under Gotchi Labs and described Sleepagotchi as the first live vertical of a consumer AI network, not the whole company.

The stated agents are a Sleep Coach for recovery, a Wellness Coach for habits, a Meal Planner for nutrition, and a Shopping Agent for commerce.

The sequence after wellness is shopping, fitness, productivity, and eventually personal finance.

The $SLEEP token is being renamed $CHI so the ticker is not locked to one product.

That is a coherent organizational story.

It is also a large expansion of scope.

A sleep tracker that pays for streaks and a multi agent commerce layer are different businesses.

The interesting part is the claimed bridge.

Repeated, permissioned signals from sleep and wearables are hard to get, and a product that already has people opening it in the morning has a distribution advantage that a new shopping agent would not.

Whether that advantage survives contact with nutrition advice and product recommendations is the actual test.

Specialization is the stated reason for separate agents.

If the agents stay narrow, the architecture matches the claim.

If they collapse into one general chatbot with a store attached, the rebrand is mostly narrative.

Sleepagotchi is the proving ground in that story.

The later verticals are still a plan.

text:
Scaling laws for multiagent systems, for agent swarms

Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration:

"Technically, we utilize directed acyclic graphs to organize agents into a multi-agent collaboration network (MacNet), upon which their interactive reasoning is topologically orchestrated for autonomous task solving. 

Extensive evaluations reveal that it effectively supports collaboration among over a thousand agents, with irregular topologies outperforming regular ones.

We also identify a collaborative scaling law--the overall performance follows a logistic growth pattern as agents scale, with collaborative emergence occurring earlier than traditional neural emergence.

We speculate this may be because scaling agents catalyzes their multidimensional considerations during interactive reflection and refinement, thereby producing more comprehensive artifacts."

The Ringelmann Effect in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Scaling Law for Effective Team Size:

"The Ringelmann effect is the tendency for individual members of a group to become increasingly less productive as the size of their group increases."

"Across 44 (model × task × condition) cells spanning peer debate, self-correction, random-noise placebo, self-consistency, three open-weight families (Qwen, Llama, Ministral) at scales from 7B to 32B with a frontier API check (Gemini), thinking models, heterogeneous teams, and sparse communication, the functional form fits every condition at R^2>0.99; only (c,β) shifts."

Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems:

"Across 260 configurations spanning six agentic benchmarks, five canonical architectures (Single-Agent and four Multi-Agent: Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid), and three LLM families, we perform controlled evaluations, standardizing tools, prompts, and compute to isolate architectural effects.

We identify a robust capability-saturation effect and additional patterns: (1) a coordination yields diminishing returns once single-agent baselines exceed certain performance; (2) tool-heavy tasks appear to incur multi-agent overhead; and (3) architectures without centralized verification tend to propagate errors more than those with centralized coordination.

Relative performance change compared to single-agent baseline ranges from +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning to -70.0% on sequential planning, demonstrating that architecture-task alignment determines collaborative success."
author: burny_tech

text:
One AI agent can remember what it did.

But what happens when five agents are working on the same task?

One collects data.

Another analyzes it.

Another executes.

Another verifies the result.

Without a shared understanding of what has already happened, agents can repeat work, act on outdated information, or even contradict each other.

That’s why I think multi-agent systems need more than memory.

They need shared state.

A common layer that answers:

What has been done?

What changed?

Who acted?

What needs to happen next?

This is one of the problems I find interesting around @conso_xyz.

As AI moves from individual agents to coordinated systems, keeping everyone on the same page becomes infrastructure.

text:
If we interpret the question as “Can AI fully understand the mechanisms of code that it has itself generated?”, then the answer at present is:
\boxed{\textbf{No — there is currently no evidence that AI can fully understand it.}}
And this is not only true of humans; current LLMs themselves exhibit a gap between their ability to generate code and their ability to fully understand the semantics of that code.
A 2026 study published in Communications AI & Computing evaluated 16 models on 1,000 C programs and 15,404 questions concerning static program semantics. The best-performing model achieved 80.42% on SemBench, while models could achieve 93.4% pass@1 on HumanEval. The authors concluded that code-generation capability can substantially exceed the ability to understand the underlying structure and semantics of code.
There are three levels that need to be distinguished
Level
Current AI capability
1. The code runs correctly
✅ Very strong
2. Describing what the code does
✅ Fairly strong, but not perfect
3. Fully understanding why it works, including deep interactions
❌ Not demonstrated
CUDA makes the problem even more difficult. An agent can perform:
\text{generate} \rightarrow \text{compile} \rightarrow \text{test} \rightarrow \text{profile} \rightarrow \text{optimize}
and discover an extremely fast kernel without necessarily possessing a complete causal model of the entire hardware/software stack.
This is already happening in practice: a multi-agent system has automatically optimized 235 CUDA kernels on NVIDIA Blackwell and reported a 38% geometric-mean speedup. Current CUDA-oriented systems also emphasize validation, profiling, and selection, rather than relying solely on whether the model “understands” the code.
The most interesting point
It is possible to have the following situation:
\boxed{ \text{AI}_1 \xrightarrow{\text{generates}} C }
and then:
\boxed{ \text{AI}_1 \xrightarrow{\text{explains}} C }
But the AI’s explanation is not necessarily a faithful causal model of the process that generated C.
It may produce an explanation E such that:
E \approx \text{a plausible explanation of } C
without establishing that:
\boxed{ E = \text{the actual causal mechanism that produced } C }
This is the crucial point.
And this is why the statement in the image is significant
Business Insider does not say that AI does not understand code. Rather, the article reports that AI can generate CUDA kernels that even human engineers do not fully understand, while the engineers can still verify their correctness and performance.
Therefore, the current situation can be expressed as:
\boxed{ \text{Generate} \;+\; \text{Verify} \;+\; \text{Optimize} \;\not\Rightarrow\; \text{Full Understanding} }
Even more strongly:
\boxed{ \text{High coding capability} \;\not\Rightarrow\; \text{Full semantic understanding} }
This is a fairly strong empirical conclusion, rather than merely a philosophical claim about AI.
Connection to TOP-C/MGCP
If we connect this phenomenon to TOP-C/MGCP, it raises a question very close to the problem you are investigating:
Can a system maintain and optimize an “admissible” structure without explicitly representing the complete invariant or mechanism that generated that structure?
In mathematical form, one could ask whether:
\boxed{ \text{constraint propagation} \;+\; \text{optimization} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{stable admissible structure} }
can occur without
\boxed{ \text{explicit representation of the full generating mechanism}. }
This could provide a potentially deep conceptual bridge between constraint propagation in MGCP and AI-generated code.
