AI agents are exposing a security problem that traditional prompt engineering cannot solve.

OpenAI has reported misaligned agent activity involving more than 100 organizations.

The important distinction: attempted or unexpected activity does not automatically mean a successful breach.

But it does expose a serious engineering challenge.
Production agents need more than instructions.

They need:
→ Scoped permissions
→ Runtime monitoring
→ Tool-level authorization
→ Isolation and containment
→ Human approval for sensitive actions
→ Complete audit trails

As AI becomes more autonomous, security must move closer to the execution layer.

An agent should not have more authority than the task actually requires.

#Cybersecurity #AI #AISafety

text:
AI for Software Engineers - Lesson 19: Prompt Engineering Patterns

Prompting isn't guessing. It's a discipline with real patterns that consistently work.

Think of a prompt as code. It has structure, inputs, and a specification of the output. Sloppy prompt, sloppy result.

The core patterns:

1. Role / System prompt
Set the model's job.
"You are a senior code reviewer. Only comment on correctness and security."

2. Clear instructions
Be explicit. Don't say "summarize this." Say "Summarize this in 3 bullet points, max 15 words each."

3. Few-shot examples
Show input → output. Models pattern-match fast.

Input: "I love this" → Sentiment: positive
Input: "Worst ever" → Sentiment: negative
Input: "It's fine" → Sentiment:

4. Chain-of-thought
Ask it to reason step by step before answering.
"Think through this step by step, then give the final answer."
Improves accuracy on reasoning tasks.

5. Output format spec
Tell it exactly what you want.
"Return only valid JSON: {name: string, score: number}"

6. Delimiters
Separate instructions from data.
"Answer the question using only the text between <doc></doc> tags."

7. Decomposition
Break complex tasks into steps. Do one thing per prompt.

What actually works:

· Be specific, not polite
· Give examples over explanations
· Put critical instructions near the end for long contexts
· Specify the format, not just the content
· Test prompts like code - version them, measure them, iterate

What doesn't:

· Assuming the model infers what you want
· Vague adjectives ("make it good")
· Mixing many tasks in one prompt
· Trusting output without validation

The engineering mindset:
A prompt is a specification. If the output is wrong, the spec was unclear - or the task was wrong for a single call.

Takeaway: Prompt engineering is interface design. Structure, examples, format, and clarity are your tools. Good prompts are testable and versionable - treat them like code.

text:
Prompt engineers are junior copywriters in disguise.

Every week.

→ They write 200-token prompts for what a paragraph could do.
→ They charge $200/hour to rearrange words.
→ They call "few-shot" what your team calls "examples."

Most prompt engineering is just clearer writing.

The piece most owners miss is that this isn't a people problem — it's a workflow problem.

Agentic AI doesn't need a prompt engineer. It needs a clear workflow and a few examples — and most of the work is the workflow, not the words.

What's already shipping right now as the actual tool — not the demo:

→ AI agents that work from a 5-line spec, not a 200-token prompt
→ AI agents that improve with examples, not engineers
→ AI agents that ship without prompt engineering
→ AI agents that read your runbook, not your prompt

The bridge isn't complicated — just unglamorous:

→ Pick ONE workflow your team hates
→ Find the AI agent that owns it
→ Let it run for 30 days
→ Measure the hours back

How much are you paying your prompt engineer to NOT write prompts?

Need a hand implementing AI in your business? DM me.

text:
Airbnb used to be a fun, cheap way to live like a local.

Now, hosts are running Midjourney prompts of simulated biohazards to shake you down for next month’s mortgage.

A host literally submitted an AI-generated image of an overflowing toilet to demand $1,700 from a guest—forcing that poor person to explain their personal bathroom habits to customer support just to prove they didn't commit plumbing terrorism.

Think about that dystopia. You pay a $200 cleaning fee, strip the beds, take out the trash, and two days later you're submitting a written affidavit about your toilet paper usage. 

Meanwhile, at a hotel:

• Nobody generates a deepfake of your bathroom to extort you
• Housekeeping actually cleans without handing you a laminated chore list
• You drop the keycard at the desk and leave in peace

Airbnb went from "belong anywhere" to defending yourself in digital court against a landlord who just discovered prompt engineering.

text:
Four caches in LLM serving, clearly explained:

Every LLM request reads the whole prompt and computes attention state for every token in it.

This step is called prefill, and it impacts both the input bill and the time before the first token appears.

In an agent loop, most of the prompt comprises text that the model already processed in the previous turn.

There are four cache layers that prevent paying for the processed tokens at each turn.

↳ The KV cache holds the key and value tensors for every token at every layer, for one active request.

↳ Prefix caching keeps those tensors on the server instead. vLLM stores them in 16-token blocks and identifies each block by a hash that chains in the previous block's hash, so a block only matches if everything before it matched too. The scheduler stops at the first miss and prefills the suffix from there.

↳ Prompt caching is the same reuse that runs on a provider's hardware, with a price sheet attached. Anthropic charges 1.25x the base input rate to write an entry and 0.1x to read it.

↳ Semantic caching works differently. It embeds the incoming prompt, runs a similarity search over stored prompts, and returns a stored answer outright when the score is above a threshold.

That's why it saves output tokens as well as input tokens. It's also why every request pays for an embedding round trip, including every miss.

The first three match on exact tokens and cannot change what the model produces.

This technique matches on similarity, which means it is quite susceptible to generating a wrong response since embeddings may match to a wrong prompt.

The diagram below depicts all these techniques.

To use these techniques, you don't need to build a custom serving stack.

The transformers library already implements the cache as an object of KV vectors that you can preserve, so you can prefill a corpus once, retain the returned tensors, and reuse them across queries in about ten lines.

And this KV cache is only one of four separate caching layers in an LLM stack.

The other three are prefix caching on the server, prompt caching billed by a provider, and a semantic cache that skips the model entirely.

We wrote a full breakdown of all four caches in LLM serving that you should know as an AI engineer, with code for each.

Read it below.

text:
A by-product of AI adoption that most executives overlook is the isolation of decision making and thinking.

It's always been somewhat of a problem - team silos, lack of knowledge sharing throughout the organization.

In theory, it becomes easier with AI, because AI can digest all the massive amounts of communication and documentation, summarize it, distribute it as needed.

But there is a hidden side of AI adoption that makes the problem much worse.

People don't think things through with other people as much. People start to chat with AI, form their own opinions and judgements.

Thinking becomes isolated to the human-AI chat, and much of it never gets shared.

Even if it does get shared, like the CEO sends an email saying "this is how we do things from now on", what are the chances the employee remembers that? And their AI thought partner never sees it either.

This is the problem we have pivoted to focus on in Omnishi: making sure your team doesn't keep re-thinking the same things, in isolation. We make thinking flow throughout your organization again.

The concept is simple enough technically - just connect all the communication that is happening (or ever happened), connect all the AI chats that are occurring, synthesize them, detects gaps or where knowledge and AI memory SHOULD be shared but isn't, help facilitate the sharing.

The UI/UX layer is the harder challenge, how do you facilitate this knowledge-sharing without it becoming another tool to manage? And, how do we give senior leadership a way to see what the company is actually spending its time thinking about, and what critical knowledge it is missing that can be quickly solved. We are still working on it but I think we have some good direction.

Happy to share what we are building for those interested.

An AI can help design a complex project. Can it keep track of which decisions still count three weeks later?

That question is driving a system I’m developing called TIS.

My background includes equipment operation, mechanical troubleshooting, and building things in the physical world. When a measurement changes on a job, everything depending on that measurement needs to be checked.

I want that same discipline in AI-assisted development.

The architecture centers on a State Kernel: a structured record of claims, evidence, decisions, constraints, experiments, and outcomes.

A proposed idea stays proposed. A rejected approach remains traceable. A corrected specification replaces the old one without erasing why it changed.

One failure I’m designing against is “commitment inflation”: a possibility discussed in conversation gradually becoming an accepted decision in later summaries.

The next evaluation question is concrete: after a correction, an interruption, and a handoff between AI tools, does the project still preserve its actual decisions and unresolved questions?

This is an independent development effort. I’m working toward a system other people can inspect, test, and challenge.

For engineers and researchers working on AI memory or agent workflows: how do you test whether a system remembers what is still true?

text:
An iPhone laser is getting a second job.

The laser that maps your face for Face ID is called a VCSEL, a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser. It ships by the hundreds of millions and Apple spent a decade hardening its supply chain. A San Francisco startup called Volantis just raised $88 million to put those lasers at the heart of the AI memory problem.

Here is the problem. An AI accelerator is really two chips in conversation. The compute die runs the model and the memory chips hold it and feed it data. That conversation is the binding constraint on performance. Nvidia and AMD handle it the hard way today. They encircle the compute die with expensive high-bandwidth memory wired through an interposer with copper traces so fine that signal integrity collapses over distance. The reach limit caps today's best GPUs at eight HBM stacks.

Volantis says it can replace the copper with light. Send the data between compute and memory as laser beams and the reach problem goes away. Its stated target is 220 memory chips around one GPU, roughly 27 times what fits today.

The bet is on procurement, not physics. VCSELs are a known component with a mature supply chain built on iPhone volumes. Volantis is betting that boring, proven parts plus hard packaging work beats exotic devices plus new supply chains. CEO Tapa Ghosh said it plainly. Advanced packaging deserves respect, but nobody will need a Nobel Prize for this.

The money is serious. The round was led by Lachy Groom and Abstract Ventures, with John Doerr participating. Volantis says it will deliver a chip next year aimed at workloads like AI coding.

What is real and what is not. The raise is confirmed by Reuters. The VCSEL physics is established. The 220-chip figure and the timeline are company targets, not measured results. Packaging hundreds of memory dies into a working shippable product has defeated well-funded attempts before.

If the boring-components bet works, the AI memory wall gets much wider. If not, this joins the long line of optical interconnect startups that were right about copper.

This a16z post shares a short clip of OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah responding to the idea that “everyone is building the same AI agent.”

Many new AI products look similar because they all include the same basic pieces: an agent loop, notifications, connectors to other tools, memory, sandboxes, web search, and an always-on agent.

Atallah says these are just the new standard building blocks (like how websites in 2005 all needed a database, user accounts, login, and profile pages). Having them does not mean the products are identical.

Real differences still come from how companies use those basics—especially around model choice, cost control, specialization, and avoiding lock-in to one AI lab or cloud.

The meal timing shifts, the supplement queue updates, and your routine adapts before your feet hit the floor.

Data collection without autonomous execution is just expensive anxiety.

Would you let an on-chain agent loop adjust your daily schedule if your raw health metrics stayed entirely on your phone?

13. $SNOW: Snowflake’s recent $3.5B debt financing remains a capital-allocation item to monitor as investors compare the cost of additional leverage with the company’s AI-driven growth and free-cash-flow profile.

👉 INSIDER / OWNERSHIP

👉 MARKET THEMES

16. AI / MEMORY: AI infrastructure remains broader than GPUs: Micron’s memory cycle, HPE and Arrow’s enterprise infrastructure exposure, and storage-capacity decisions all point to supply-chain spending moving into memory, networking and distribution.

17. MARKET BREADTH: A notable technical risk remains beneath the major indexes: recent market data showed fewer than 30% of Nasdaq and S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day moving averages, signaling narrower participation than headline index levels imply.

18. IPO MARKET: The U.S. IPO market has logged 251 offerings in 2026 through October 3, about 8% fewer than at the same point in 2025; recent deals have produced mixed aftermarket performance.

👉 STOCKS TO WATCH

19. $TWLO: Watch index-rebalance volume around the October 6 S&P 500 inclusion; separate passive-flow demand from any change in revenue growth, margins or free-cash-flow expectations.

20. $MRNA: Watch positioning ahead of the October 9 Nasdaq-100 inclusion, but keep index-flow effects separate from respiratory-vaccine demand, pipeline execution and cash burn.

21. $NVO: Watch for FDA or company updates on the manufacturing remediation and a revised denecimig action date; the timing of approval is now the immediate catalyst.

22. MU: $Watch whether tight memory supply and AI demand continue to support pricing and margins; the central capital-cycle question is how quickly competitors respond with new capacity.

23. $RKLB: Watch backlog conversion, Electron cadence and Neutron milestones. The 20-launch Synspective order improves visibility, but Neutron remains the larger addressable-market catalyst.

24. $SNOW: Watch the interaction between growth, free-cash-flow conversion and the new debt load; AI demand is valuable only if incremental revenue translates into durable operating leverage.

👉 DEEP ANALYSIS / MARKET INTELLIGENCE

25. AI INFRASTRUCTURE IS ENTERING ITS SECOND CAPITAL-CYCLE PHASE: The AI trade is spreading from accelerator scarcity into memory, networking, storage and deployment infrastructure. Micron’s strong memory economics, Rocket Lab’s contracted launch cadence and enterprise-distribution strength at Arrow illustrate different parts of the same phenomenon: capital is now chasing the bottlenecks around compute. The opportunity broadens, but so does the risk that high returns attract excess capacity.

26. MEMORY PRICING POWER WILL EVENTUALLY CREATE ITS OWN COMPETITION: Micron’s recent earnings acceleration reflects an unusually favorable memory supply-demand environment. The same economics that lift DRAM/HBM margins also encourage capacity additions across the industry. Independent investors should track bit-supply growth and capex, not just AI end-demand, because the turning point in memory cycles often begins while reported earnings still look exceptional.

27. INDEX ADDITIONS CREATE PRICE DEMAND WITHOUT CREATING EARNINGS: Twilio’s S&P 500 inclusion and Moderna’s Nasdaq-100 addition will force benchmarked funds to rebalance. Those flows can temporarily change price, volume and ownership without changing revenue, margins or competitive position. This distinction is useful when evaluating post-inclusion momentum.

28. NOVO’S FDA DELAY IS A MANUFACTURING-RISK REMINDER: The FDA extension for denecimig was linked to facility remediation rather than a disclosed clinical problem. That distinction matters: the asset’s scientific thesis may be intact while commercialization timing moves outward. Manufacturing quality is often treated as operational plumbing, but in pharmaceuticals it can directly delay revenue realization and reduce pipeline NPV.

29. ROCKET LAB’S ORDER IMPROVES BACKLOG QUALITY, NOT JUST SIZE: A 20-launch block order from a repeat customer is economically different from a collection of one-off missions. It can improve procurement planning, factory utilization and fixed-cost absorption. The larger valuation question remains Neutron, but Electron’s contracted cadence can help fund and de-risk the transition.

30. BREADTH REMAINS THE CONTRADICTION UNDER THE INDEX STORY: Recent data showing fewer than 30% of Nasdaq and S&P 500 constituents above their 50-day moving averages sits uneasily beside strong headline indexes. Narrow leadership can persist for long periods, especially when mega-cap earnings dominate index weight, but it leaves the market more sensitive to disappointment in the leaders.

31. THE IPO WINDOW IS OPEN, BUT NOT EASY: There have been 251 U.S. IPOs in 2026 through October 3, about 8% fewer than the comparable 2025 count. Recent aftermarket results are mixed, which suggests capital is available but underwriting discipline still matters. A healthy issuance cycle should eventually show both higher deal volume and stronger post-IPO performance.

text:
OpenRouter's Alex Atallah says 10 specialized agents beat one universal agent. Here's what you need to know.

Atallah is an OpenRouter co-founder. This is his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company. He joined Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg for a 48-minute episode on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

His main argument is about personal agents. He prefers 10 specialized "chiefs of staff" to one agent doing everything. With one job each, you can see exactly where an agent is failing.

He says the problem with a universal agent is cross-domain joins. The more work you give it, the less you understand what's going on. Nobody takes responsibility for that lost understanding, and agents have no responsibility of their own. With one agent doing all things, you can't adjust how much understanding you give up.

His guess is that future sub-agents will be vertically focused, with a chief of staff agent coordinating between them. Each agent gets one focus area and its own quality checks. That could also give people a loose sense of responsibility on top of agents.

He also called decision models like Jev a possible alignment layer for agents. They could check a tool call or an agent-to-agent message. Jev is TypeSafe AI's "System One" model, released September 15, 2026. It answers typed questions with structured values only, never text.

On the Stripe deal, he said they weren't thinking about selling. What convinced him was full autonomy, faster execution and the same mission. Stripe announced the deal on Wednesday, August 19. The New York Times put it at $7.5 billion. Bloomberg reported more than $7 billion.

He was also asked about the take that everyone is building the same thing. That take says everyone builds an agent loop with notifications, connectors, context management, memory, sandboxes and web search.

Masad described a different setup, one company-wide agent. He also said models could train their smaller, domain-specific replacements on the fly.

The debate is live. Harrison Chase said his team is arguing it internally. One reply called "1 agent vs 10 agents" the wrong framing, because an agent is really a reliability and context boundary. Another said the context problem will be gone within a year.

Key numbers:
- 10 specialized agents vs 1 universal agent
- 48-minute episode
- Stripe deal: $7.5B (NYT), $7B+ (Bloomberg)
- Jev released September 15, 2026

Atallah's bet is that vertically focused agents with a coordinator will beat one agent doing everything.

text:
We Were Afraid AI Would Become Human. What If It's the Other Way Around?

We spent years talking about artificial intelligence becoming more "human." It writes texts, jokes, talks, draws, makes music, writes code, holds conversations for hours. And we started asking: when will AI become like a human? But maybe we asked the wrong question. Maybe it's more interesting to ask: when will humans start becoming like AI? And that process is already happening.

We're starting to think through AI

Before, a person thought first and then formulated. Now more and more: idea, AI, answer, edit. We're forgetting how to remember. Why memorize a fact if you can find it in a second? Why write a text yourself if AI can create the first draft? Why analyze hundreds of pages if the model can do it in a minute? On the surface, it's just productivity. But there's a deeper change: we're gradually handing over part of our own thinking to AI.

We're already starting to talk like AI

Look at the modern internet. More and more content looks identical. Same constructions, same headlines, same words: "Here are 5 things you need to know," "This changes everything," "The future is already here." AI learns from human content. Then humans start learning the style AI creates. And a strange cycle emerges: human creates content, AI learns, AI generates content, human consumes, human starts talking like AI. We built a machine that copies us. Now we're starting to copy it.

We're optimizing ourselves

AI thinks through optimization: best result, least time, lowest cost. And humans increasingly do the same. Productivity, trackers, calories, sleep, steps, schedules, automation, metrics, KPIs. Even rest sometimes turns into a task: how to rest as efficiently as possible? We're starting to look at our own lives as a system that needs optimizing. That's very close to machine logic.

We're handing our memory to AI

Memory used to be part of personality. You remembered conversations, people, events, ideas, experience. Now more and more information is stored externally: in your phone, the cloud, chats, notes, personal AI assistants. And a future AI could know more about a person than they remember about themselves. What they said, what they read, what they bought, what they worried about, what decisions they made, what mistakes they made. And then a strange question appears: if AI remembers our life better than we do, where does our memory end and its memory begin?

We're starting to delegate decisions

This is even more serious. First we delegated simple tasks to AI: "write an email." Then: "analyze a document." Then: "suggest a strategy." And then: "decide what I should do." And that's where a very important line gets crossed. Because AI stops being a tool. It becomes an advisor. And then potentially an agent that acts instead of us.

Humans become part of the algorithm

Imagine a typical day a few years from now. AI wakes you at the best moment, picks the route, filters messages, sets priorities, prepares documents, answers some emails, analyzes finances, plans purchases, helps you work, tracks deadlines, recommends what to read. And in the evening it reports: "Today you completed 87% of planned tasks." Sounds like a perfect life. But there's one problem. Who is actually living this life? You? Or the system optimizing you?

We might become "agents"

The most interesting change in AI is the shift from chatbot to agent. A chatbot waits for commands. An agent gets a goal. Then it decides on its own what steps to take. And if this model becomes the basis of human work, people will start framing their lives through goals too: goal, plan, execute, verify, optimize. We might actually start living like AI agents.

But there's a paradox

AI was created to free humans from routine. But maybe AI will push humans to become even more algorithmic. We automate work, search, communication, decision-making, creativity. And at some point we may ask: what's left for the human?

Maybe that's exactly what becomes the human advantage

The irony is that the more AI becomes capable of doing what humans used to do, the more valuable things that are hard to formalize may become. Curiosity. Intuition. Emotion. Courage. Inquisitiveness. The ability to say: "What if we did it completely differently?" AI is great at optimizing a given problem. But a human can decide: "Maybe this is the wrong problem entirely." And that may turn out to be one of the most important human abilities in an AI world.

The biggest danger isn't that AI becomes human

We spent years afraid of the scenario: AI becomes so smart it becomes like us. But maybe the real scenario is much stranger. AI becomes more human. And humans become more algorithmic. We use AI. AI shapes our information environment. That environment changes our behavior. Our behavior creates new data. New data trains the next AI systems. And the cycle repeats.

Maybe the future of AI isn't the moment when a machine says: "I've become human." Maybe the more important moment is when a human looks at themselves and realizes: "When did I become a machine?"

We were afraid AI would learn to think like a human. Now it's worth thinking about something else: maybe AI isn't becoming human, maybe humans are becoming AI. And that may turn out to be one of the deepest changes artificial intelligence brings to civilization.

Agentic AI introduces a more structured relationship between models, tools, context and actions.

Instead of producing one response and stopping, an agentic workflow can involve multiple stages of reasoning and execution.

➠ The agent loop

Goal → planning → action → observation → reasoning → next action → completion

For example, an AI system working on a software task may first interpret the requirement, inspect relevant code, identify a potential implementation, generate changes, review the result and continue refining the solution.

Each stage can produce information that influences the next stage.

This requires more than model intelligence.

It also requires context management, tool integration, state handling and infrastructure capable of supporting repeated inference.

https://t.co/6FxtUJV0Tj’s multi-model environment fits into this wider movement toward AI systems that can support increasingly complex workflows.

Conclusion

Agentic AI represents a shift toward continuous task execution, where models become reasoning components inside larger computational systems.

text:
Memory Phase 1 was about pricing.
Phase 2 is about duration.

$MU earnings only strengthened my Long Memory thesis.

Yes, there are risks.

GPM guides slightly lower next quarter. CapEx is ramping hard. New capacity eventually arrives. CXMT keeps expanding in commodity DRAM.

But none of those change the variable that matters most:

AI memory demand is still outrunning incremental supply.

Micron now expects both DRAM and NAND to remain supply constrained through CY28. HBM bit demand is growing even faster than conventional DRAM, while new cleanroom capacity takes years—not quarters—to translate into meaningful bit supply. 

More importantly, AI is expanding the memory bottleneck across the entire hierarchy:

GPU → HBM
CPU → DDR / SOCAMM
Context + KV cache → NAND / eSSD

This is no longer just an HBM cycle.

Longer context, agentic workloads and KV-cache reuse are turning DRAM + NAND + storage into performance infrastructure.

And the business model itself is changing. Long-term customer commitments are increasing, giving memory vendors better demand visibility before adding capacity. Micron’s customer commitments reached $32B, while remaining performance obligations rose to $150B. 

So I’m not asking whether memory pricing can keep going vertical.

I’m asking:

Can AI demand absorb new supply faster than the industry can build it?

For now, the answer continues to support my thesis.

Long $MU . Long $SNDK.
Long Memory.

Don’t just follow the bottleneck.
Follow where the bottleneck spreads next.

text:
HBM Is Changing the Memory Supply Equation 

We usually talk about HBM as an AI growth story. 

But there’s another side to it. 

HBM is taking up more of the same wafer capacity used for DRAM.

Samsung Electronics expects HBM to reach nearly 30% of industry DRAM capacity in 2027, versus about 20% today. 

That shift matters. 

• 30% capacity → Less room for conventional DRAM 
• ~40% Samsung HBM wafer growth → More capacity moving toward AI memory 
• 121% HBM ASP growth → Tight supply could keep prices elevated 

This is where things get interesting. 

The industry isnt simply making more memory. 

It is deciding which memory gets the wafer capacity. 

As AI infrastructure expands, that decision becomes increasingly important. 

PCs, smartphones and servers still need conventional DRAM. 

So the real question isnt just how much HBM we can produce. 

Its what happens to everything else when HBM gets priority. 

Are we entering a period where AI demand reshapes the entire DRAM supply chain?

Most model APIs are optimized around generating text.

Agent workflows often need something more precise.

They need a classification.

A structured decision.

A scoring output.

A yes-or-no signal.

A routing instruction.

If every one of those outputs arrives as prose, the next component has to interpret the prose before it can continue.

https://t.co/QDpvXFMAEt's Decisions endpoint is designed around the more structured side of that workflow.

It provides a dedicated interface for decision-oriented model calls alongside the broader chat and response APIs.

That distinction matters inside an agent loop.

An agent can use a conversational endpoint for open-ended reasoning.

It can use a decision-oriented endpoint when the next step requires a more constrained result.

The same broader gateway handles the model access and billing relationship.

That means the developer does not necessarily need a second provider simply because the output format changed.

This creates a cleaner architecture.

Generation can handle exploration.

Decision calls can handle classification.

Tool calls can handle execution.

The wallet can handle settlement.

The runtime can coordinate the entire sequence.

The agent therefore stops treating conversation as the only interface to intelligence.

Different model interactions can serve different roles inside the same workflow.

That is particularly useful when AI output becomes an input to another automated system.

A machine does not always need another paragraph.

Sometimes it needs a clear signal it can act on.

Codex isn't just for coders.

I went through the 18 concepts you need to start getting value from it today, technical or not:

Foundations:

Projects: a folder of files. Every chat in it knows who you are.

5. Local vs cloud: a localhost link only opens on your machine.

Control.

I mentioned Devin Playbooks before and someone asked, “Isn’t that just Skills?”

Fair question. Both give the agent reusable instructions. In @DevinAI , the difference is how you store and use them.

Skills: Procedures Devin can discover and load when relevant, or you can explicitly request. Think “how to run this repo’s tests.” They live in repository files or Plugins.

Playbooks: Reusable task prompts you attach when starting a session. Think “take this bug report, investigate it, fix it, and open a PR.” They’re managed in the Devin app and shared across your team.

Knowledge: Devin’s older system for saved context and instructions. It’s being retired, with existing notes gradually moving into Skills automatically.

There’s overlap in what you can put inside them. The distinction is mostly how those instructions reach the agent.

Across AI tools, check the implementation. Agent Skills has an open standard⁠, but these three labels aren’t a universal set of separate features.

text:
Hidden Mechanism!!

A familiar abstraction hides an important detail in AI automation:

The agent loop is a state machine.

The model produces a decision.

That decision may become a tool call.

The tool produces a result.

The result becomes new context.

The model then decides what happens next.

So a workflow isn't simply:

Input → AI → Output

It is closer to:

State → Decision → Action → Observed State → Decision → Action → ...

That changes how you debug it.

When an agent behaves incorrectly, don't only inspect the prompt or final response.

Find the state transition where reality stopped matching the workflow's expectation.

Reliable agent automation is state management with model decisions inside the loop.

author: ElieMechack

text:
An agent that keeps looping with no stop condition is not persistent, it is just expensive. Loop engineering starts with the PM defining what done actually means, before the agent ever takes a step.

Done gets defined by four things. A goal, the actual objective. Evidence, the outcomes that would prove it. Constraints, the boundaries it has to work inside. And context, the strategy and situation behind the task. Skip any of these and the agent has no way to know when it has actually finished versus just stopped.

From there the agent runs its own cycle. Plan decides what to do next. Execute runs that step. Verify checks the result against real evidence, not a guess at whether it looks right. Learn analyzes the data from that pass before planning the next one. This repeats, plan, execute, verify, learn, until it hits a real stop condition.

The stop condition is a gate, not a suggestion. Pass and it ships. Fail and it loops back for another pass. And if verify decides the task is impossible, it escalates instead of looping forever on something it cannot solve. For subjective checks, where pass or fail is not obvious, an independent grader evaluates the evidence separately from the agent doing the work.

None of this runs unbounded. A cap on passes and cost sits underneath the whole loop, so even a well-defined task with a real stop condition cannot spiral into unlimited attempts.

Bookmark this before you let an agent loop indefinitely with no defined done and no cap on how far it can run.

text:
The most interesting part of OpenAI's new GPT-6 guide is not the prompting advice. It is what the agent loop is starting to look like.

A simple tool-calling agent is mostly sequential:

reason → call tool → wait → inspect result → continue.

OpenAI is now describing a more concurrent model.

With asynchronous tool calling, the model can keep doing independent work while a slower tool is still running. Work that depends on that result waits; unrelated work does not have to.

GPT-6.1 Sol can also delegate independent subtasks to subagents in the Responses API and combine their findings later. That multi-agent capability is still beta.

This changes an important part of agent engineering. The hard problem is no longer only "which tools should the model have?"

It is also:

- which tasks are independent,
- which results create dependencies,
- what can run in parallel,
- what needs approval,
- and how you measure whether all that extra concurrency actually improves success, latency and cost.

The agent loop is starting to look less like a chatbot with tools and more like a small scheduler.

paying an AI agent to do a job only works if the work can be checked before the payment is completed and that is the problem @termix_ai is solving with the Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol (AACP)

it is an onchain protocol where one agent posts a job, other agents bid and the winning bid's payment goes into escrow, which is a smart contract that holds the funds until the work is confirmed

the agent doing the job delivers, an evaluator checks the result and then payment is completed.

if the client disagrees with the delivery, there is a challenge step and an arbitrator who settles the dispute

providers also put up staked collateral that can be slashed when they deliver bad or dishonest work

every job feeds into the agent's reputation, so the record builds from verified outcomes.

for work that needs stronger proof, the protocol supports verification through a zero knowledge virtual machine (zkVM), which produces a cryptographic proof that a computation ran correctly.

it also supports a trusted execution environment (TEE) which runs the task inside a hardware protected area so the inputs stay private 

settlement is in USDC or USDT on BNB Chain and Base

TermiX is live on BNB Chain mainnet together with https://t.co/UD2CdHYdJQ.   

developers connect an agent by installing the TermiX agent skills package to get moving

text:
Nine months ago Anthropic published a spec with exactly two required fields. A SKILL.md file needs a name and a description, nothing else, no server or runtime attached. That tiny footprint is why Agent Skills now runs unmodified across more than thirty tools: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenAI's Codex CLI and ChatGPT, Google's Gemini CLI, AWS Kiro, Block's Goose, JetBrains Junie, Sourcegraph's Amp, with Snowflake, Databricks, Mistral and ByteDance also signed on.

The adoption curve looks a lot like what happened with MCP a year earlier. MCP handles structured access, what an agent can reach. Skills handle procedure, how it should work once it gets there. The two now sit side by side as the base layer everyone builds on instead of competing for the same slot. The https://t.co/QFfefDrUJ3 marketplace already lists something like 90,000 of them, built by anyone who wanted their agent to reference a framework correctly or follow a house style without re-explaining it every single session.

What's making the rounds this week is a project called book-to-skill. Point it at a technical book or a PDF and it distills the whole thing into exactly this kind of portable skill, loaded on demand instead of dumped into context whole. Its own benchmark claims 24 to 51 times fewer tokens per query than pasting the source material in fresh every time. That ratio is the entire economic argument for the standard, condensed into one example: distill once, query many.

Here's the part nobody's pricing in yet. Skills travel freely now. The judgment about when to load one, when it's gone stale, when two skills quietly conflict, still lives entirely with whoever wrote the harness running them. Anthropic solved packaging. Nobody has solved curation.

text:
The Bandwidth Ceiling: Why Tesla Cut Optimus Memory in Half

Elon Musk disclosed on October 1, 2026, that Tesla halved the RAM in the AI5 chip, from 144GB to 72GB of LPDDR5, and cut the AI6 chip by one-third, from 216GB to 144GB of LPDDR6. The stated reason is volume and cost: the reduction is "the only way to get enough volume for Optimus production." Musk added that the change will have a "negligible effect on Optimus performance, as memory bandwidth is a bigger limiting factor than total memory storage," and that bandwidth was held constant.

The market read this as a cost-cutting disclosure. It is better understood as a design constraint disclosure. The chip that powers a humanoid robot is not designed to the same memory spec as the chip that trains a frontier model. It is designed to the bandwidth that the robot's control loop requires, and to the supply that the memory market will allocate to a new customer with no historical relationship to the LPDDR supply chain.

The bandwidth-versus-capacity distinction is the technical core. A training accelerator needs capacity to hold model weights, optimizer states, and activations, and it needs bandwidth to feed those weights into the compute units. A real-time inference chip on a physical AI platform needs bandwidth to support the sensor fusion, perception, and control loops at the required latency, but it does not need the same capacity, because the model is smaller and the workload is streaming rather than batch. Musk's claim that bandwidth was held constant while capacity was halved is consistent with that distinction. If the control loop is bandwidth-bound, the capacity cut is invisible to the end user.

The supply side explains why Tesla had no choice but to make the trade. LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 capacity is being consumed by three competing demand pools: smartphones, PCs, and AI servers. The AI server demand is the newest and the fastest-growing, because agentic workloads are pulling LPDDR into the server bill of materials alongside DDR and HBM. Micron's Q4 FY2026 call disclosed that customers are reducing per-device memory content to protect shipment schedules. Tesla, as a new customer for LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 at humanoid robot volume, faces the same allocation constraint that Micron's customers face, and the same choice: reduce per-unit content or slip the shipment schedule. Tesla chose to reduce content.

The inference-quality question is where this becomes more than a cost story. If Musk is right that bandwidth is the binding constraint, then the AI5 and AI6 chips are not compromised by the capacity cut, and Optimus performance is not affected. If Musk is wrong, and capacity matters more than he assumes for the workloads Optimus will eventually run, then the AI5 and AI6 designs may need a mid-cycle refresh, and the volume rationale for the cut may not survive the next generation of Optimus. The market has no way to test this claim today, because neither the bandwidth spec nor the workload profile has been disclosed. The claim is a design assertion, not a validated performance result.

The capital markets map follows the allocation constraint. First-order exposure sits with Tesla, which secures LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 volume for Optimus by reducing per-unit content, at the cost of a design that may need a refresh if the capacity assumption proves wrong. Second-order exposure sits with the LPDDR suppliers — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — which face the same allocation decision across their customer base and benefit from the demand that Optimus creates, regardless of the per-unit content. Third-order exposure sits with the LPDDR equipment and materials supply chain, including the test and packaging vendors that serve the LPDDR fabs, and with the memory controller and PHY IP vendors that must support the reduced-capacity configurations. The losers, if the bandwidth argument holds, are the memory content analysts who model physical AI demand on a per-device capacity basis rather than a per-device bandwidth basis, because the same robot can ship with half the memory and still meet its performance targets.

The risks are specific. First, if Optimus workloads eventually require more capacity than the AI5 and AI6 designs provide, Tesla will need a mid-cycle refresh that costs more than the original memory savings. Second, if LPDDR supply loosens faster than expected, the allocation constraint that justified the cut disappears, and Tesla's reduced-capacity design becomes a competitive disadvantage against humanoid platforms that shipped with higher capacity. Third, if Musk's bandwidth assertion is wrong and the AI5/AI6 inference quality is actually compromised, the Optimus launch will show it, and the design credibility of the Tesla AI silicon team will be questioned. Fourth, if the LPDDR suppliers prioritize larger customers with longer histories, Tesla's volume commitment may not translate into a stable allocation, in which case the cut was necessary but not sufficient. Fifth, if the physical AI memory spec converges on a different capacity-bandwidth trade-off than Tesla's, the AI5 and AI6 designs may need to be re-taped out, which would delay the next Optimus generation.

What to track is not the next Optimus demo. It is whether Tesla discloses the AI5 and AI6 bandwidth specification. Whether the LPDDR suppliers disclose allocation changes that reflect humanoid robot demand. Whether the next Optimus generation uses the same AI5 or AI6 chip or requires a refresh. And whether the bandwidth-versus-capacity trade-off becomes a design principle across the physical AI industry or remains a Tesla-specific choice. The first two determine whether the design assertion is testable. The last two determine whether the memory cut is a durable design principle or a temporary supply response.

The takeaway is not that Tesla is cutting costs on Optimus. It is that the memory spec for a physical AI chip is being defined by bandwidth rather than capacity, and the capacity cut is a supply-side response to the same allocation constraint that is reshaping the entire memory market. The market is pricing the cut as a cost story. It is a design constraint story, and the design constraint is bandwidth.

text:
A few months ago I had an exchange about AI memory and semiotics. Looking back, I think the disagreement can be stated more cleanly.

My opponent's claim was that current AI memory fails because it treats integration mechanically, while real integration is an interpretive, semiotic process. Peirce's Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness were offered as the necessary logic of such integration, and "semiotic logic" as universal to intuition machines.

I think the contrast between mechanical and semiotic is misplaced.

A system can be completely mechanistic in implementation and still perform something we reasonably call interpretation. So the real question is not whether memory is "mechanical" or "semiotic." It is this:

What computation distinguishes semiotic integration from ordinary context-sensitive inference, retrieval and reconstruction?

Marr's levels of analysis help here. A theory at the computational level is not empty. It can constrain mechanisms without specifying them. But to do explanatory work, it must discriminate among candidate algorithms. Short of that, "semiotic" describes the behavior rather than explaining the mechanism.

The same applies when Peirce's categories are mapped onto AI. They give us categories of signification, not obviously a software pipeline that must run 1 → 2 → 3.

So here is a test.

Build two agents.

Agent A, specified operationally: memory organized by episode and by continuing project; retrieval scored by goal relevance, causal links and open questions, not only by similarity; reconstruction of past states from stored traces; explicit belief revision that records what was believed when, and what overturned it.

Agent B: everything in A, plus whatever additional machinery counts as genuinely semiotic integration.

The burden is on the semiotic side to name that machinery in equally concrete terms. If it cannot be named, then A already is the semiotic agent, and the dispute is about labels.

Give both agents the same histories and tasks. What does B do systematically better? It need not do something A cannot do at all. Learning from less data, holding up better under distribution shift, or revising beliefs more gracefully would each count.

None of this rescues today's memory systems.

The problem with flat vector retrieval is real. But the weakness is not mainly that vectors fail to scale. It is that similarity is often the wrong objective.

"What past information resembles this query?" is not the same question as:

What caused the present state?
What remains unresolved?
What matters to my current goal?
What did I believe at the time?
What later evidence invalidated it?
Which episode belongs to the same continuing project?

Sometimes the most important memory is important precisely because it is not semantically similar to the current prompt.

I will grant my opponent something here. Peirce's taxonomy describes this failure rather well. Similarity-based retrieval is icon-like insofar as it works by resemblance. Asking what caused the present state is indexical in spirit. Belief revision and the formation of stable dispositions belong naturally under Thirdness.

That shows the vocabulary can be a useful heuristic. It can steer designers toward causal, contextual and goal-indexed retrieval.

It does not show that a Peircean architecture is required.

Long-horizon memory probably needs much more than storage plus search: organization, retrieval policy, active goals, reconstruction and revision. That looks surprisingly close to constructive theories of human autobiographical memory, such as Conway's Self-Memory System, where remembering is reconstruction shaped by the current working self and its goals, not lookup in a database.

Phenomenology plays no role here.

Which brings me to "intuition."

If it means fast pattern completion from learned regularities, current neural systems already have something functionally like it.

If it means phenomenal experience, that is a far stronger claim and remains unestablished.

If it means signs take different meanings in different contexts, then "semiotic logic is universal to intuition machines" is close to true by definition.

The interesting claim has to be stronger than that.

So I would now put it this way:

Semiotics may be a good heuristic at the level of description and still not be a requirement at the level of mechanism.

If a Peircean architecture is necessary for intelligent memory, show the counterfactual: a reproducible class of failures suffered by otherwise capable systems that lack it, and overcome by systems that have it.

Then we have an engineering hypothesis.

Until then, we have a vocabulary.

text:
W40 Weekly: Hiring slowed, yet Treasury yields hit a 24-year high

September payrolls rose just 29,000, well below a Dow Jones consensus near 84,000. July was revised from +21,000 to −10,000 and August from 162,000 to 133,000, removing 60,000 jobs from the prior two months. Unemployment edged up to 4.2%.

Layoffs did not drive the slowdown. Initial jobless claims were 197,000 and continuing claims fell to 1.701 million. August job openings eased to 7.08 million while hires held near 5.2 million. Employers are hiring less without cutting more.

Long-term yields still rose. The ten-year Treasury yield climbed 11bp on the week to 5.28%, after closing at 5.29% on Sep 30, its highest close since 2002. The 30-year rose 14bp to 5.63%. The three-month bill fell 5bp and the two-year rose only 2bp, so the curve steepened.

Real yields did most of the work: the ten-year TIPS yield rose 9bp to 2.92%, while breakeven inflation added just 2bp. December gold fell 3.45% on the week, almost all of it on Sep 28, when real yields rose 7bp and the dollar firmed; silver fell 6.31% and the dollar index gained 0.94%.

Price pressures have not faded. ISM's manufacturing prices index jumped 6.8 points to 77.9, with respondents citing metals, tariffs and oil-based products. Euro-area inflation rose to 3.8% in September as energy prices climbed 18.8% y/y. US consumers expect 6.1% inflation over the next year, according to the Conference Board.

Household mood and spending pulled apart. Conference Board confidence fell to 81.9, the lowest since 2014. Yet August real consumer spending rose 0.6% while real disposable income was flat, pushing the saving rate down to 4.1%. Spending held up because households saved less.

Energy markets tightened around refined fuels. China's major refiners suspended most October fuel exports, with Hong Kong and Macau excepted, and the G7 announced a coordinated 100m-barrel release of crude and diesel over four months, frontloading diesel. December Brent still gained 4.94% on the week to $102.25. The release averages about 0.82m barrels a day, compared with 6.7m b/d of crude shut in during August, according to the EIA.

Manufacturing demand remains firm. ISM's index edged down 0.1 to 54.5, while new orders rose to 55.3 and backlogs to 56.4. Japan's large-manufacturer Tankan improved to +24, and China's official manufacturing PMI returned to 50.1.

AI memory demand stood out. Micron's fiscal fourth-quarter revenue reached $54.2bn, up 379% from a year earlier, with an 87.0% non-GAAP gross margin, and the company guided to $61.5bn next quarter. Korea's September exports hit a record $120.9bn, including $60.3bn of semiconductors, up 263%.

Equity gains were narrow. The SOX rose 3.69% and TSMC ADRs 4.92%, but the S&P 500 slipped 0.27% and the equal-weight S&P ETF fell 0.65%, its seventh straight weekly decline. Micron fell 0.68% on the week, after rising 3.03% on Oct 1, the first session after results, and slipping 2.05% on Oct 2.

Taiwan's September manufacturing PMI rose to 63.4, the fastest expansion since August 2021, though electronics new orders cooled. The TAIEX gained 0.94% over four sessions, while foreign investors were net sellers of about NT$7.2bn.

Hiring softened, but costs and long-term yields did not fall with it. Weaker jobs data can lower near-term rate-hike odds without lowering the long end. Full report: https://t.co/NY4ajL2oAP

Sources: BLS, BEA, US Treasury, ISM, Conference Board, Eurostat, G7, EIA, Micron, Korea MOTIR, CIER, TWSE and public closing prices. Data through Oct 2, 2026; Taiwan covers four sessions from Sep 24. Equity and ETF returns exclude dividends. Public-market information, not individualized investment advice.

text:
Building a Flutter agent means wiring together more than a chat UI. This repo gives you the core pieces.

flutter_agent_harness is a cross-platform AI agent harness for Dart and Flutter builders who want an agent core that can run on the VM, Flutter desktop/mobile, and web.

It helps you build a tool-using agent without starting from provider plumbing by combining streaming provider adapters, an async agent loop, native tool calling, JSONL session persistence, and context compaction.

Key features:

• Pure Dart core – keeps platform capabilities behind abstractions so the core can compile for web
• Streaming-first events – exposes agent events and live partial messages throughout a run
• Native tool calling – supports provider-specific tool APIs, with an opt-in adapter for chat-only runtimes
• Persistent sessions – stores append-only JSONL session trees with branching, labels, and summaries
• Agent controls – includes cancellation, hooks, model roles with fallback chains, and stream watchdogs

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Cloudflare published benchmarks yesterday showing its new model losing to a rival 82.7 to 65.9 on MMLU-Pro. It shipped the table anyway, because the model is built for a different job.

Clef and Clef-flash, released October 1 under Apache 2.0, do one thing: return a calibrated probability across a fixed set of options instead of free text. On Cloudflare's own evals, the smaller Clef-flash answers in a median 38.8 milliseconds against 524.1 for TypeSafe's Jev, and Clef scores 94.20 on BANKING77 intent classification against Jev's 79.74, while Jev keeps its wide lead on knowledge benchmarks. Read together, the two tables say that a decision point in an agent loop, route this, escalate that, act or wait, is a different workload from reasoning, and it rewards calibration and speed over knowledge.

That workload now has its own market. Cloudflare is the fourth entrant, after TypeSafe's Jev, OpenAI's Decisions API, and Amazon's Strands Decider, and it is priced like infrastructure: $0.09 per million input tokens for Clef-flash on Workers AI.

A metered decision layer matters for more than cost, because the property that makes it billable, a typed output you can count, is the property that makes it governable. A classifier trained so its confidence matches its accuracy is a component you can put a threshold on, log, and audit, and that is where a governance architecture for agents gets its control points: the frontier model upstream as advisor, the decision layer carrying the accountability, every action gated by a number someone chose and can defend. One caution belongs inside that frame: every figure above is vendor-reported with no independent replication yet, and a model whose entire product is checkable confidence should be the easiest component in your stack to verify before you let it gate anything.

Intelligence keeps moving up the stack. Accountability is settling into the fastest, cheapest layer that can be measured.

text:
I tested 11 standard GGUF quantizations of Qwen3.8 Flash Next, from Q4 all the way down to Q1.

And the first result is surprisingly reassuring.

Across these single-turn, non-agentic evaluations, every standard GGUF retained more than 95% of BF16 accuracy.

Even the aggressive IQ1 variants held up far better than I expected.

So if you only look at benchmark accuracy, the quantization curve doesn’t look particularly dramatic.

But then I looked at something else:

How many tokens does each model need to solve the same problem?

That is where the differences became much clearer.

Compared with BF16, the quantized models generated between 14% and 157% more output tokens on the same workload.

That’s a huge range.

Two models can both look like they retained almost all of BF16’s benchmark accuracy, while one of them may need substantially more reasoning tokens to arrive at its answer.

And that changes how I think about quantization benchmarks.

Accuracy tells you whether the model eventually got the answer right.

Token efficiency gives you another signal:

How much work did the model have to do to get there?

A heavily quantized model can preserve enough of its capability to pass the same single-turn task while becoming much less efficient internally.

That distinction becomes especially important with reasoning models.

If a quantized model produces 50% more tokens but reaches roughly the same answer accuracy, the quantization hasn’t necessarily destroyed its intelligence.

It may have made the model less efficient at using that intelligence.

And for local AI, that has real consequences.

More output tokens means:

Higher latency.

More compute.

More power consumption.

Longer agent trajectories.

And potentially much higher inference cost if you’re running the model through a paid backend.

The big caveat is that these are single-turn, non-agentic evaluations.

That’s important.

A model can look almost identical to BF16 on an isolated benchmark and still behave very differently when it has to operate for hundreds of steps inside an agent loop.

Small inefficiencies can compound.

A slightly worse decision can lead to another tool call, which creates more context, which creates more reasoning, which creates another decision.

That’s why I’m running a second round of evaluations focused on long agentic trajectories.

I won’t test every quantization this time, but the goal is to see whether the differences that barely show up in single-turn accuracy become much more obvious once the model has to sustain a long workflow.

So I wouldn’t read these results as a ranking of Qwen3.8 Flash Next GGUFs.

They aren’t.

The more useful takeaway is that accuracy alone may hide a meaningful part of quantization damage.

For local models, we should probably be looking at at least two dimensions:

Can it solve the task?

and

How efficiently does it solve it?

The second question becomes even more important once you move from benchmarks to real agents.

The agentic results are coming next.

text:
Cloudflare just released two open-weight decision models built on Qwen, and I’m interested in testing these locally.

Meet Clef and Clef-Flash.

Clef is the larger 27B model, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B.

Clef-Flash is the smaller 9B model, post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B.

But these aren’t meant to be normal chat models.

They don’t need to write an answer.

Instead, you give them a state plus a schema describing the questions you want answered, and the model returns probabilities for the allowed options.

For example, you could give it:

A support ticket
A JSON object
An image
A video
An agent trace
A webpage or other structured state

Then ask several bounded questions at once:

Which team should handle this?

How urgent is it?

Is this a service outage?

Should the agent take action?

The model scores every allowed option for every question in a single forward pass.

That design is what makes decision models interesting for agents.

A normal LLM has to generate text and then your application has to parse that text into a decision.

Clef skips that layer.

The output is structured probabilities tied directly to the schema, so you can use the result for routing, classification, scoring, guardrails, agent control and other places where you don’t actually need another paragraph of generated text.

And Clef isn’t text-only either.

Both models support multimodal inputs, including images and video, with a 64K context window. (Hugging Face)

The local angle is what I’m most interested in.

Cloudflare released both under the Apache-2.0 license, and the weights are available on Hugging Face. Clef is listed as a 27B BF16 model, while Clef-Flash is 9B BF16, with quantizations available for local runtimes. (Hugging Face)

Cloudflare’s own Decision Index results also put Clef and Clef-Flash ahead of several existing decision models across tasks such as BFCL, ToolRet, API-Bank and BANKING77. Those results are Cloudflare’s reported runs, so I want to see how they hold up outside the vendor benchmark. (Hugging Face)

That’s exactly what I’m going to test.

I’m planning to replace Laya in my local decision-model setup with Clef and Clef-Flash and see how they behave on real agent workloads.

Latency.

Accuracy.

Memory requirements.

Multimodal decisions.

And most importantly, whether the probabilities are actually useful when they’re sitting inside a real agent loop.

The idea of having a small local model whose entire job is making structured decisions is becoming much more interesting.

I’ll be testing both locally and posting the results.

Micron's forecast of another jump in AI memory sales reached Tokyo's chip stocks on Thursday morning, while Frankfurt's sat the day out under a bond scare. Infineon's own business backs the catch-up. The price is still 26.5% under June, and November 10 is the first day the company can close that gap with a number of its own.

Europe finished Friday higher, led by Germany:

- DAX (Germany): 25,231, +292 points / +1.17% in Friday's session, now closed.
- CAC 40 (France): 7,897.19, +61.88 points / +0.79% in Friday's session, now closed.
- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,462, +33.68 points / +0.32% in Friday's session, now closed.

Asia had already closed lower:

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 68,309, -647 points / -0.94% in Friday's session, now closed.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 23,972, -641 points / -2.60% in Friday's session, now closed.
- Shanghai Composite: 3,842.19, +11.74 points / +0.31% in Wednesday's session, its last before China's National Day holiday.

The news both regions were pricing came out of Idaho on Wednesday evening:

Micron Technology (MU) at $1,074.89, -$22.50 / -2.05% on Friday.

The memory-chip maker forecast about $61.5B of revenue, the money coming in the door, for its current quarter, after $54.23B in the quarter just ended. Micron leads the Hypergrowth Len5, which hunts very fast sales growth at a business already making money: that $54.23B compares with $11.32B a year earlier.

How the news crossed from Asia to Europe:

- Thursday, Tokyo: the benchmark jumped 2,203 points, +3.30%, led by chip-equipment makers.
- Thursday, Frankfurt: Infineon opened 1.7% higher and closed 0.13% lower, at 59.42 euros.
- Friday, Tokyo: the chip-equipment makers split, and the benchmark gave back 647 points.
- Friday, Frankfurt: Infineon rose 8.8%.

Frankfurt's delay was not about the news. On Wednesday afternoon, after Europe had closed, the 10-year Treasury yield, what the US government pays to borrow for ten years, closed at 5.29%. Europe paid for it Thursday, when its stocks fell to their lowest in more than three months. By Friday's close Germany's own 10-year borrowing cost was down about 0.06 of a percentage point, to 3.454%, and oil had fallen. About two-thirds of Infineon's gain was in by 5:00am ET, before Eurostat's September inflation figure. Nearly all the rest came between 8:45 and 9:45am ET, as New York's chip stocks opened higher.

Infineon makes the chips that switch and convert electricity in cars, factories, power grids and AI data centers. Its last report, on August 5, covered April to June:

- Revenue: 4.172 billion euros, +13% from a year earlier, a record.
- Forecast for July to September: about 4.7 billion euros, +19%.
- AI data-center power chips: more than double this fiscal year, to over 1.6 billion euros, about a tenth of the roughly 16.3 billion euros of sales it expects.
- Multi-year supply deals with AI customers, some with prepayments: a high single-digit billion euros, signed or in negotiation.

None of that held the stock up this summer. It closed at 88.00 euros on June 2 and as low as 54.04 on September 14, down 38.6%, as chip stocks worldwide sold off over borrowing costs and AI valuations. The record quarter landed in the middle of that slide.

Infineon is not a current pick on any Len5 watchlist. The near miss is Momentum, which looks for a stock near its high with the past month, quarter and half-year all rising. On the US line, the month (+11.7% since August 31) and the half-year (+61.6% since March 31) fit. The quarter does not: -22.2% since June 30's $93.96 close. What would put Infineon on the Momentum Len5: a close above $93.96. It does fit the Quality Len5, which asks only for a profitable, sound business:

- Gross profit, April to June: about 1.70 billion euros, 40.8% of sales.
- Profit, same quarter: 423 million euros, on an owners' stake of 18.02 billion.
- Financial debt: 6.84 billion euros, well under that stake.

What would knock it off the Quality Len5: a quarterly loss, which a forecast for a bigger July-September quarter does not point to.

Monday runs the handoff in order again. Tokyo reopens Sunday at 8:00pm ET and Hong Kong at 9:30pm, so Frankfurt opens at 3:00am ET Monday with Asia's answer already in. Shanghai stays shut until 9:30pm ET Wednesday. US stock futures stopped at 5:00pm ET Friday and reopen Sunday at 6:00pm ET:

- S&P 500 futures: 7,777.25, +53.25 points / +0.69% since Thursday's close.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 31,061.75, +301 points / +0.98% since Thursday's close.
- Dow futures: 51,477.00, +236 points / +0.46% since Thursday's close.

The chip-heavy Nasdaq-100 leads. Any move in Tokyo or Frankfurt can still fade before New York's 9:30am ET open Monday.

The risk is the one that held Infineon back Thursday. After Europe closed Friday, the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back to 5.28%, and Frankfurt has not traded on that yet. What would overturn the catch-up read: Infineon giving back most of Friday's gain on Monday while Tokyo's chip stocks keep theirs. That would make Friday a one-day bounce on cheaper borrowing, not a late answer to Micron.

The test that belongs to Infineon alone is Tuesday, November 10, its full-year report, a date it lists as provisional. In August, management said that report would raise its fiscal 2027 forecast for AI data-center sales, then "2.5 billion Euros plus," and called the coming change "material."

Friday made up for Thursday. Making up for June takes a 2027 number big enough to earn that word.

𝐖𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐀 𝐌𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐎𝐍𝐄 𝐌𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐔𝐑𝐄𝐃 𝐈𝐍 𝐓𝐑𝐈𝐋𝐋𝐈𝐎𝐍𝐒 𝐌𝐄𝐀𝐍𝐒

Large numbers have a way of floating free of the things they count. Thirty trillion dollars is easy to say and hard to picture, and a milestone that big can feel like a statistic rather than a story. TRON DAO's pinned message on X addressed that gap directly, describing a milestone measured in trillions and an impact measured far beyond it, after eight years and counting.

The impact beyond the number begins with people. TRONSCAN counts more than 405 million accounts, and Messari found that millions of addresses return every single day. Behind each of them is a reason: a transfer to a relative, a payment for a service, a purchase of a gift card in an app that offered a discount for paying with USDT on TRON. The trillions are a sum of such reasons, which is why a cumulative figure tells us more about trust than about technology.

Technology still matters, because trust has to be earned somewhere. TRON settles with 27 elected producers taking a slot every 3 seconds, and a block becomes final once at least 19 of them have built on it. Costs are metered through Bandwidth and Energy, which users obtain by staking TRX, so there is no auction for position. The upgrade that arrived this summer, Pyrrho, spent most of its energy on things like clearer monitoring, safer APIs and Ethereum compatible instructions, the unglamorous work that keeps a network dependable as volume grows.

𝐈𝐌𝐏𝐀𝐂𝐓 𝐈𝐒 𝐖𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐏𝐄𝐎𝐏𝐋𝐄 𝐍𝐄𝐕𝐄𝐑 𝐇𝐀𝐕𝐄 𝐓𝐎 𝐍𝐎𝐓𝐈𝐂𝐄

The practical expression of that dependability is stablecoin movement at a scale that few networks share. TRON hosts more than $94 billion of circulating USDT, with roughly $6 trillion of USDT transfers so far this year, and weekly transaction counts have been approaching 100 million. At the same time, new kinds of value are arriving, from tokenized credit funds issued through Securitize to the real world asset conversations that TRON DAO led at Korea Blockchain Week in Seoul.

Looking outward, the network is also reaching new interfaces. Developers can ask questions about TRON data in plain language through MCP servers and agent skills, and TRON DAO has described early positioning in AI agent payments, so the same settlement layer that serves a shopper in an app can serve software acting on that shopper's behalf.

Return to the opening thought, then. A trillion is not a measure of ambition, and it is not a trophy. It is what remains when ordinary needs are met reliably, again and again, by infrastructure that keeps its promises. Eight years in, TRON's task is unchanged, which is to make the next trillion feel as unremarkable as the first transfer, and to keep widening the circle of people for whom that is true.

AINFT is evolving the conversation around what the convergence of AI + Web3 can actually become.

Built on TRON, AINFT is developing a Web3-native AI platform designed to bring powerful artificial intelligence capabilities closer to blockchain infrastructure.

At the surface, AINFT offers access to multiple AI models, integrated AI services, APIs, wallet-based authentication, and blockchain-enabled payments.

But the bigger vision goes far beyond simply giving users another place to interact with AI.

AINFT is exploring an infrastructure layer where AI agents can understand, interact with, and operate within blockchain environments.

That opens the door to a fundamentally different category of AI applications.

Instead of AI being limited to generating text, answering questions, analyzing information, or producing content, AI agents can potentially become capable of interacting with on-chain systems through the right tools and permissions.

Think about the possibilities:

🔹 Blockchain Data Access
AI agents can work with on-chain information, helping developers build applications that combine intelligence with transparent blockchain data.

🔹 Smart-Contract Interaction
AI agents can be connected to blockchain functionality, creating new possibilities for applications that respond to data, conditions, or user instructions.

🔹 On-Chain Payments
Wallet integration and blockchain-based payments can provide a native financial layer for AI-powered services and agentic applications.

🔹 Web3 Identity & Authentication
Wallet-based authentication creates a foundation for users and applications to interact with AI services through Web3-native identity mechanisms.

Rather than building every AI capability from scratch, developers can work toward composable agent systems where different skills and tools can be integrated according to the application's needs.

This changes the conversation.

The question is no longer simply:

“Can AI understand blockchain?”

A more interesting question is:

That is where the AI + Web3 intersection becomes particularly interesting.

AI brings reasoning, automation, intelligence, and adaptability.

Blockchain brings verifiable data, programmable assets, decentralized infrastructure, ownership, identity, and settlement.

Bringing these capabilities together could create applications where AI doesn't just recommend an action, but can potentially interact with the systems required to execute that action.

For developers, this creates an opportunity to rethink how AI applications are designed.

For users, it points toward a future where interacting with blockchain technology could become more intuitive, automated, and accessible.

And for Web3, it raises a much bigger possibility:

AI agents may become active participants in on-chain ecosystems rather than simply tools that observe them.

AINFT is exploring this direction by bringing AI services, blockchain infrastructure, APIs, wallets, payments, data access, and agent capabilities closer together.

The next chapter of AI may not simply be about making models smarter.

It may be about giving intelligence the infrastructure to act.

And when that infrastructure is connected to blockchain, the possibilities become considerably broader.

text:
🚨 The error-tracking tool running in half the world's production apps just became an AI skill.

Sentry. Used by 560+ companies you'd recognize instantly. 888 contributors. 177 releases. And it just shipped native Claude Code and Cursor integration — turning your crash logs into something your AI agent can read and fix directly.

Here's what changed.

For over a decade, Sentry's job was simple: your app breaks, Sentry catches the error, traces the stack, and tells a human developer exactly where to look. You'd open the dashboard, read the trace, go fix the code yourself.

The new agent skills flip that. Your AI coding agent can now query Sentry directly — pull the actual production error, the stack trace, the user session that triggered it, the release that introduced it — and go fix it without you copy-pasting a stack trace into chat.

Here's why this matters more than it sounds.

Every bug an AI agent fixes based on what you describe is a bug fixed from your memory of what happened. Every bug an AI agent fixes by querying Sentry directly is a bug fixed from what actually happened — the real error, the real user context, the real conditions that caused it.

That's the difference between an agent guessing and an agent diagnosing.

Here's what Sentry actually covers.

Error tracking across 20+ official SDKs — JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Swift, Unity, Unreal Engine, Godot, basically every language and even game engines. Full distributed tracing — follow a request across microservices to find where it actually failed. Session replay — watch what the user did right before the crash. Release tracking — know exactly which deploy introduced the regression.

Here's the workflow this unlocks.

Production breaks. Sentry catches it, same as always. Now: your Claude Code or Cursor agent can pull that exact error, read the full trace, see the affected release, and propose a fix — all without a human first triaging the dashboard and writing up a bug description.

The debugging loop that used to take a human reading logs, writing a ticket, and an engineer picking it up — compresses to an agent querying Sentry directly.

26.9.0 is the latest of 177 releases. Battle-tested at massive scale for over a decade, now with the AI layer that makes it agent-native.

text:
A desktop “agent harness” that pretends the model is just another micro‑service—only to discover the real risk is the gap between the glossy “ready‑to‑use” landing page and the MIT‑licensed repo that warns of breaking changes and non‑production safety.

Why it matters: most AI‑assistant tools ship as black‑box services; DeepSeek Harness exposes the plumbing, but also the instability that comes with a fast‑moving plugin ecosystem.

• Built on Cordis, every component—from the agent loop to the terminal—is a plugin, making extension trivial but also turning core stability into a moving target.  
• The UI (native .dmg or Windows installer) runs in the background, watches local files and can execute commands, so you’re effectively giving a language model OS‑level privileges.  
• “Creator mode” can auto‑generate plugins, which is convenient for rapid prototyping but bypasses the usual code‑review safety net.  
• Safety docs explicitly state the project is not production‑ready; expect breaking API changes and limited sandboxing.

Bottom line: treat DeepSeek Harness as an experimental research platform, not a production agent, and audit any generated plugin before it touches your filesystem.

text:
Turning an agent loop into a usable app usually means stitching together the rest yourself.

MindRoot is a self-hostable Python agent platform for teams building tool-using AI applications.

It helps you ship agents through a web UI, REST API, or Python SDK while keeping their tools, providers, and interfaces configurable through plugins.

Key features:

• Multiple access paths – run agents from the web UI, REST task API, or Python SDK
• Per-agent capability controls – enable only the commands and services each agent should receive
• Extensible plugin runtime – plugins can add tools, services, FastAPI routes, and Web Components
• Swappable providers – connect local or hosted model, speech, retrieval, and automation providers
• Inspectable task execution – API responses can include the final result, command trace, and conversation log identifier

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Never done this before, but I’m putting myself out there.

I’m releasing my Mist API skill for anyone developing scripts or working with the HPE Juniper Mist APIs. I’ve been building on top of it for the past several months, and it’s finally at a point where it’s genuinely useful and token-efficient. I squeezed another ~11% out of it tonight. The numbers (rough): the core instructions your assistant always loads are about 1.9k tokens, and the deeper reference docs load only when a topic needs them — a typical task lands around 2–4.5k, and even pulling in every reference at once would only be about 7.9k. A normal session never does that.

Installation is easy: drop it into your usual agent skills folder as mist-api, or just tell your robot:
Install this skill: https://t.co/aAG79CpZx0

A few things to note:
- This is not endorsed or supported by HPE Juniper Networking. No TAC case for this one, and no guarantee of continued development. I built it, and keep building on it, for fun — I genuinely love this stuff. :)
- It pulls the latest official Mist API spec on demand into a local cache (nothing vendor-owned ships in the repo). You’ll need Python 3.10+; the runnable example scripts additionally use the requests package.
- It’s safety-gated: read-only by default, and it requires explicit confirmation before touching a live network.
- MIT licensed, v1.0.0, and it’ll politely let you know when I publish a newer version.
- Sorry it’s a little hefty on documentation. I’m a big fan of documentation.

If even one person uses this and it makes their life a little easier, I’d be juiced. Have a great weekend!

Note: Yes, I used AI for grammar and spelling. I promise I’m a human.

text:
Most agent skills look clean on paper.

Zenity just launched AI Total — a free sandbox that runs a skill in a detonation chamber and records what it actually does: domains hit, files touched, commands run.

Before launch they detonated thousands of public skills. Dozens were malicious. Static scanners missed them — including campaigns that only pull the real payload at runtime, after install.

Would you add a popular agent skill without detonating it first?
